Now we modify the example in the previous bullet point by translating the functions in the previous bullet point by arbitrary integers. Specifically, for k a nonnegative integer and $m \in \mathbf { Z }$ , define $e _ { k , m } \colon { \mathbf { R } } \to { \mathbf { F } }$ by 

$e _ { k , m } ( x ) = { \left\{ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & { { \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } } x \in \left[ m + { \frac { n - 1 } { 2 ^ { k } } } , m + { \frac { n } { 2 ^ { k } } } \right) } \\ { - 1 } & { { \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } } x \in \left[ m + { \frac { n - 1 } { 2 ^ { k } } } , m + { \frac { n } { 2 ^ { k } } } \right) } \\ { 0 } & { { \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } } x \not \in [ m , m + 1 ) . } \end{array} \right. }$ for some odd integer $n \in [ 1 , 2 ^ { k } ]$ for some even integer $n \in [ 1 , 2 ^ { k } ]$ 

Then $\{ e _ { k , m } \} _ { ( k , m ) \in \{ 0 , 1 , \dots \} \times \mathbf { Z } }$ is an orthonormal family in $L ^ { 2 } ( \mathbf { R } )$ 

This example illustrates the usefulness of considering families that are not sequences. Although $\{ 0 , 1 , \ldots \} \times \mathbf { Z }$ is a countable set and hence we could rewrite $\{ e _ { k , m } \} _ { ( k , m ) \in \{ 0 , 1 , \dots \} \times \mathbf { Z } }$ as a sequence, doing so would be awkward and would be less clean than the $e _ { k , m }$ notation. 

The next result gives our first indication of why orthonormal families are so useful. 

Proof Suppose $\{ \alpha _ { j } \} _ { j \in \Omega }$ is a family in F. Standard properties of inner products show that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \left\| \sum_ {j \in \Omega} \alpha_ {j} e _ {j} \right\| ^ {2} & = \left\langle \sum_ {j \in \Omega} \alpha_ {j} e _ {j}, \sum_ {k \in \Omega} \alpha_ {k} e _ {k} \right\rangle \\ & = \sum_ {j, k \in \Omega} \alpha_ {j} \overline {{\alpha_ {k}}} \langle e _ {j}, e _ {k} \rangle \\ & = \sum_ {j \in \Omega} | \alpha_ {j} | ^ {2}, \end{array}
$$

as desired. 

Suppose Ω is a finite set and $\{ e _ { j } \} _ { j \in \Omega }$ is an orthonormal family in an inner product space. The result above implies that if $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { j \in \Omega } \alpha _ { j } e _ { j } = 0 } \end{array}$ , then $\alpha _ { j } = 0$ for every $j \in \Omega$ 

Linear algebra, and algebra more generally, deals with sums of only finitely many terms. However, in analysis we often want to sum infinitely many terms. For example, earlier we defined the infinite sum of a sequence $g _ { 1 } , g _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . in a normed vector space to be the limit as $n \to \infty$ of the partial sums $\scriptstyle \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { n } g _ { k }$ if that limit exists (see 6.40). 

The next definition captures a more powerful method of dealing with infinite sums. The sum defined below is called an unordered sum because the set Γ is not assumed to come with any ordering. A finite unordered sum is defined in the obvious way. 

8.53 Definition unordered sum; $\sum_{k\in\Gamma}f_k$ Suppose $\{f_k\}_{k\in\Gamma}$ is a family in a normed vector space $V$ . The unordered sum $\sum_{k\in\Gamma}f_k$ is said to converge if there exists $g\in V$ such that for every $\varepsilon>0$ , there exists a finite subset $\Omega$ of $\Gamma$ such that $\left\|\boldsymbol{g}-\sum_{j\in\Omega'}f_j\right\|<\varepsilon$ for all finite sets $\Omega'$ with $\Omega\subset\Omega'\subset\Gamma$ . If this happens, we set $\sum_{k\in\Gamma}f_k=g$ . If there is no such $g\in V$ , then $\sum_{k\in\Gamma}f_k$ is left undefined. 

Exercises at the end of this section ask you to develop basic properties of unordered sums, including the following: 

• <sup>Suppose</sup> $\{ a _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Gamma }$ is a family in R and $a _ { k } \geq 0$ for each $k \in \Gamma$ . Then the unordered sum $\textstyle \sum _ { k \in \Gamma } a _ { k }$ converges if and only if 

$$
\sup \left\{\sum_ {j \in \Omega} a _ {j}: \Omega \text {   is   a   finite   subset   of   } \Gamma \right\} <   \infty .
$$

Furthermore, if $\textstyle \sum _ { k \in \Gamma } a _ { k }$ converges then it equals the supremum above. If $\textstyle \sum _ { k \in \Gamma } a _ { k }$ does not converge, then the supremum above is ∞ and we write $\textstyle \sum _ { k \in \Gamma } a _ { k } = \infty$ (this notation should be used only when $a _ { k } \geq 0$ for each $k \in \Gamma )$ . 

8.55 

Suppose $\{ a _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Gamma }$ is a family in R. Then the unordered sum $\textstyle \sum _ { k \in \Gamma } a _ { k }$ converges if and only if $\textstyle \sum _ { k \in \Gamma } \left| a _ { k } \right| < \infty$ . Thus convergence of an unordered summation in R is the same as absolute convergence. As we are about to see, the situation in more general Hilbert spaces is quite different. 

Now we can extend 8.52 to infinite sums. 

8.54 linear combinations of an orthonormal family
Suppose $\{e_{k}\}_{k\in\Gamma}$ is an orthonormal family in a Hilbert space V. Suppose $\{\alpha_{k}\}_{k\in\Gamma}$ is a family in F. Then
(a) the unordered sum $\sum_{k\in\Gamma}\alpha_{k}e_{k}$ converges $\Longleftrightarrow \sum_{k\in\Gamma}|\alpha_{k}|^{2}<\infty$ .
Furthermore, if $\sum_{k\in\Gamma}\alpha_{k}e_{k}$ converges, then
(b) $\left\|\sum_{k\in\Gamma}\alpha_{k}e_{k}\right\|^{2}=\sum_{k\in\Gamma}|\alpha_{k}|^{2}.$ 

Proof First suppose $\textstyle \sum _ { k \in \Gamma } \alpha _ { k } e _ { k }$ converges, with $\Sigma _ { k \in \Gamma } \alpha _ { k } e _ { k } = g$ . Suppose $\varepsilon > 0$ Then there exists a finite set $\Omega \subset \Gamma$ such that 

$$
\left\| g - \sum_ {j \in \Omega^ {\prime}} \alpha_ {j} e _ {j} \right\| <   \varepsilon
$$

for all finite sets $\Omega ^ { \prime }$ with $\Omega \subset \Omega ^ { \prime } \subset \Gamma$ . If $\Omega ^ { \prime }$ is a finite set with $\Omega \subset \Omega ^ { \prime } \subset \Gamma$ , then the inequality above implies that 

$$
\| g \| - \varepsilon <   \left\| \sum_ {j \in \Omega^ {\prime}} \alpha_ {j} e _ {j} \right\| <   \| g \| + \varepsilon ,
$$

which (using 8.52) implies that 

$$
\| g \| - \varepsilon <   \left(\sum_ {j \in \Omega^ {\prime}} | \alpha_ {j} | ^ {2}\right) ^ {1 / 2} <   \| g \| + \varepsilon .
$$

Thus $\begin{array} { r } { \| g \| = \left( \sum _ { k \in \Gamma } \lvert \alpha _ { k } \rvert ^ { 2 } \right) ^ { 1 / 2 } } \end{array}$ , completing the proof of one direction of (a) and the proof of (b). 

To prove the other direction of (a), now suppose $\textstyle \sum _ { k \in \Gamma } \vert \alpha _ { k } \vert ^ { 2 } < \infty$ . Thus there exists an increasing sequence $\Omega _ { 1 } \subset \Omega _ { 2 } \subset \cdots$ of finite subsets of Γ such that for each $m \in { \mathbf { Z } } ^ { + }$ 

$$
\sum_ {j \in \Omega^ {\prime} \backslash \Omega_ {m}} | \alpha_ {j} | ^ {2} <   \frac {1}{m ^ {2}}
$$

for every finite set $\Omega ^ { \prime }$ such that $\Omega _ { m } \subset \Omega ^ { \prime } \subset \Gamma$ . For each $m \in { \mathbf Z } ^ { + } .$ , let 

$$
g _ {m} = \sum_ {j \in \Omega_ {m}} \alpha_ {j} e _ {j}.
$$

If $n > m$ , then 8.52 implies that 

$$
\| g _ {n} - g _ {m} \| ^ {2} = \sum_ {j \in \Omega_ {n} \backslash \Omega_ {m}} | \alpha_ {j} | ^ {2} <   \frac {1}{m ^ {2}}.
$$

Thus $g _ { 1 } , g _ { 2 } , \ldots .$ is a Cauchy sequence and hence converges to some element $g$ of V. 

Temporarily fixing $m \in { \mathbf Z } ^ { + }$ and taking the limit of the equation above as $n \to \infty$ we see that 

$$
\| g - g _ {m} \| \leq \frac {1}{m}.
$$

To show that $\Sigma _ { k \in \Gamma } \alpha _ { k } e _ { k } = g$ , suppose $\varepsilon > 0$ . Let $m \in { \mathbf Z } ^ { + }$ be such that $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 2 } { m } < \varepsilon . } \end{array}$ Suppose $\Omega ^ { \prime }$ is a finite set with $\Omega _ { m } \subset \Omega ^ { \prime } \subset \Gamma$ . Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left\| g - \sum_ {j \in \Omega^ {\prime}} \alpha_ {j} e _ {j} \right\| \leq \| g - g _ {m} \| + \left\| g _ {m} - \sum_ {j \in \Omega^ {\prime}} \alpha_ {j} e _ {j} \right\| \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \frac {1}{m} + \left\| \sum_ {j \in \Omega^ {\prime} \setminus \Omega_ {m}} \alpha_ {j} e _ {j} \right\| \\ \qquad = \frac {1}{m} + \Big (\sum_ {j \in \Omega^ {\prime} \setminus \Omega_ {m}} | \alpha_ {j} | ^ {2} \Big) ^ {1 / 2} \\ <   \varepsilon , \end{array}
$$

where the third line comes from 8.52 and the last line comes from 8.55. Thus $\Sigma _ { k \in \Gamma } \alpha _ { k } e _ { k } = g .$ , completing the proof. 

## 8.56 Example a convergent unordered sum need not converge absolutely

Suppose $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \mathbf { Z } ^ { + } }$ is the orthogonal family in $\ell ^ { 2 }$ defined by setting $e _ { k }$ equal to the sequence that is 0 everywhere except for a 1 in the $k ^ { \mathrm { { t h } } }$ slot. Then by 8.54, the unordered sum 

$$
\sum_ {k \in \mathbf {Z} ^ {+}} \frac {1}{k} e _ {k}
$$

converges in $\ell ^ { 2 }$ (because $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { k \in \mathbf { Z } ^ { + } } \frac { 1 } { k ^ { 2 } } < \infty ) } \end{array}$ even though $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { k \in { \bf Z } ^ { + } } \| \frac { 1 } { k } e _ { k } \| = \infty } \end{array}$ . Note that $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { k \in \mathbf Z ^ { + } } \frac { 1 } { k } e _ { k } = ( 1 , \frac 1 2 , \frac 1 3 , \dots ) \in \overset { \cdot } { \ell } ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ 

Now we prove an important inequality. 

## 8.57 Bessel’s inequality

Suppose $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Gamma }$ is an orthonormal family in an inner product space V and $f \in V .$ Then 

$$
\sum_ {k \in \Gamma} | \langle f, e _ {k} \rangle | ^ {2} \leq \| f \| ^ {2}.
$$

Proof Suppose Ω is a finite subset of $\Gamma$ . Then 

$$
f = \sum_ {j \in \Omega} \langle f, e _ {j} \rangle e _ {j} + \left(f - \sum_ {j \in \Omega} \langle f, e _ {j} \rangle e _ {j}\right),
$$

where the first sum above is orthogonal to the term in parentheses above (as you should verify). 

```txt
Bessel's inequality is named in honor of Friedrich Bessel (1784–1846), who discovered this inequality in 1828 in the special case of the trigonometric orthonormal family given by the third bullet point in Example 8.51. 
```

Applying the Pythagorean Theorem (8.9) to the equation above gives 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \| f \| ^ {2} = \left\| \sum_ {j \in \Omega} \langle f, e _ {j} \rangle e _ {j} \right\| ^ {2} + \left\| f - \sum_ {j \in \Omega} \langle f, e _ {j} \rangle e _ {j} \right\| ^ {2} \\ \geq \left\| \sum_ {j \in \Omega} \langle f, e _ {j} \rangle e _ {j} \right\| ^ {2} \\ = \sum_ {j \in \Omega} | \langle f, e _ {j} \rangle | ^ {2}, \end{array}
$$

where the last equality follows from 8.52. Because the inequality above holds for every finite set $\Omega \subset \Gamma$ , we conclude that $\begin{array} { r } { \| f \| ^ { 2 } \geq \sum _ { k \in \Gamma } \lvert \langle f , \bar { e _ { k } } \rangle \rvert ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ , as desired. 

Recall that the span of a family $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Gamma }$ in a vector space is the set of finite sums of the form 

$$
\sum_ {j \in \Omega} \alpha_ {j} e _ {j},
$$

where Ω is a finite subset of Γ and $\{ \alpha _ { j } \} _ { j \in \Omega }$ is a family in F (see 6.54). Bessel’s inequality now allows us to prove the following beautiful result showing that the closure of the span of an orthonormal family is a set of infinite sums. 

8.58 closure of the span of an orthonormal family
Suppose $\{e_{k}\}_{k\in\Gamma}$ is an orthonormal family in a Hilbert space V. Then
(a) $\overline{\operatorname{span}\{e_{k}\}_{k\in\Gamma}}=\left\{\sum_{k\in\Gamma}\alpha_{k}e_{k}:\{\alpha_{k}\}_{k\in\Gamma}\right.$ is a family in F and $\sum_{k\in\Gamma}|\alpha_{k}|^{2}<\infty\bigg\}.$ Furthermore,
(b) $f = \sum_{k \in \Gamma} \langle f, e_{k} \rangle e_{k}$ for every $f \in \overline{\operatorname{span}\{e_{k}\}_{k \in \Gamma}}$ . 

Proof The right side of (a) above makes sense because of 8.54(a). Furthermore, the right side of (a) above is a subspace of V because $\ell ^ { 2 } ( \Gamma )$ [which equals $\mathcal { L } ^ { 2 } ( \boldsymbol { \mu } )$ , where $\mu$ is counting measure on Γ] is closed under addition and scalar multiplication by 7.5. 

Suppose first $\{ \alpha _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Gamma }$ is a family in F and $\textstyle \sum _ { k \in \Gamma } \vert \alpha _ { k } \vert ^ { 2 } < \infty$ . Let $\varepsilon > 0$ . Then there is a finite subset Ω of Γ such that 

$$
\sum_ {j \in \Gamma \backslash \Omega} | \alpha_ {j} | ^ {2} <   \varepsilon^ {2}.
$$

The inequality above and 8.54(b) imply that 

$$
\left\| \sum_ {k \in \Gamma} \alpha_ {k} e _ {k} - \sum_ {j \in \Omega} \alpha_ {j} e _ {j} \right\| <   \varepsilon .
$$

The definition of the closure (see 6.7) now implies that $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { k \in \Gamma } \alpha _ { k } e _ { k } \in \mathrm { s p a n } \left\{ e _ { k } \right\} _ { k \in \Gamma } } \end{array}$ showing that the right side of (a) is contained in the left side of (a). 

To prove the inclusion in the other direction, now suppose $f \in { \overline { { \operatorname { s p a n } \left\{ e _ { k } \right\} _ { k \in \Gamma } } } }$ . Let 

$$
g = \sum_ {k \in \Gamma} \langle f, e _ {k} \rangle e _ {k},\tag{8.59}
$$

where the sum above converges by Bessel’s inequality (8.57) and by 8.54(a). The direction of the inclusion that we just proved implies that $g \in \operatorname { s p a n } { \{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Gamma } }$ . Thus 

$$
g - f \in \overline {{\operatorname{span} \left\{e _ {k} \right\} _ {k \in \Gamma}}}.\tag{8.60}
$$

Equation 8.59 implies that $\langle g , e _ { j } \rangle = \langle f , e _ { j } \rangle$ for each $j \in \Gamma$ , as you should verify (which will require using the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality if done rigorously). Hence 

$$
\langle g - f, e _ {k} \rangle = 0 \quad \text {   for   every   } k \in \Gamma .
$$

This implies that 

$$
g - f \in \left(\operatorname{span} \{e _ {j} \} _ {j \in \Gamma}\right) ^ {\perp} = \left(\overline {{\operatorname{span} \{e _ {j} \} _ {j \in \Gamma}}}\right) ^ {\perp},
$$

where the equality above comes from 8.40(d). Now 8.60 and the inclusion above imply that $f = g \left[ \sec 8 . 4 0 ( \mathbf { b } ) \right]$ , which along with 8.59 implies that f is in the right side of (a), completing the proof of (a). 

The equations $f = g$ and 8.59 also imply (b). 

## Parseval’s Identity

Note that 8.52 implies that every orthonormal family in an inner product space is linearly independent (see 6.54 to review the definition of linearly independent and basis). Linear algebra deals mainly with finite-dimensional vector spaces, but infinitedimensional vector spaces frequently appear in analysis. The notion of a basis is not so useful when doing analysis with infinite-dimensional vector spaces because the definition of span does not take advantage of the possibility of summing an infinite number of elements. 

However, 8.58 tells us that taking the closure of the span of an orthonormal family can capture the sum of infinitely many elements. Thus we make the following definition. 

<table><tr><td>8.61 Definition orthonormal basis</td></tr><tr><td>An orthonormal family <eq>\{e_k\}_{k\in\Gamma}</eq> in a Hilbert space V is called an orthonormal basis of V if<eq>\overline{\text{span } \{e_k\}_{k\in\Gamma}} = V.</eq></td></tr></table>

In addition to requiring orthonormality (which implies linear independence), the definition above differs from the definition of a basis by considering the closure of the span rather than the span. An important point to keep in mind is that despite the terminology, an orthonormal basis is not necessarily a basis in the sense of 6.54. In fact, if Γ is an infinite set and $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Gamma }$ is an orthonormal basis of $V ,$ then $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Gamma }$ is not a basis of V (see Exercise 9). 

## 8.62 Example orthonormal bases

For $n \in { \bf Z } ^ { + }$ and $k \in \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ , let $e _ { k }$ be the element of $\mathbf { F } ^ { n }$ all of whose coordinates are 0 except the $k ^ { \mathrm { { t h } } }$ coordinate, which is 1: 

$$
e _ {k} = (0, \dots , 0, 1, 0, \dots , 0).
$$

Then $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \{ 1 , \dots , n \} }$ is an orthonormal basis of $\mathbf { F } ^ { n }$ 

Let $\begin{array} { r } { e _ { 1 } = \big ( \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 3 } } , \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 3 } } , \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 3 } } \big ) , e _ { 2 } = \big ( - \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 2 } } , \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 2 } } , 0 \big ) } \end{array}$ , and $\begin{array} { r } { e _ { 3 } = \big ( \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 6 } } , \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 6 } } , - \frac { 2 } { \sqrt { 6 } } \big ) } \end{array}$ . Then $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \{ 1 , 2 , 3 \} }$ is an orthonormal basis of $\mathbf { F } ^ { 3 }$ , as you should verify. 

The first three bullet points in 8.51 are examples of orthonormal families that are orthonormal bases. The exercises ask you to verify that we have an orthonormal basis in the first and second bullet points of 8.51. For the third bullet point (trigonometric functions), see Exercise 11 in Section 10D or see Chapter 11. 

The next result shows why orthonormal bases are so useful—a Hilbert space with an orthonormal basis $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Gamma }$ behaves like $\ell ^ { 2 } ( \Gamma )$ 

8.63 Parseval's identity
Suppose $\{e_{k}\}_{k\in\Gamma}$ is an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space V and $f,g\in V$ . Then
(a) $f=\sum_{k\in\Gamma}\langle f,e_{k}\rangle e_{k};$ (b) $\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\Gamma}\langle f,e_{k}\rangle\overline{\langle g,e_{k}\rangle};$ (c) $\|f\|^{2}=\sum_{k\in\Gamma}|\langle f,e_{k}\rangle|^{2}.$ 

Proof The equation in (a) follows immediately from 8.58(b) and the definition of an orthonormal basis. 

<table><tr><td>8.64 Definition separable</td></tr><tr><td>A normed vector space is called separable if it has a countable subset whose closure equals the whole space.</td></tr></table>

To prove (b), note that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \langle f, g \rangle & = \Big \langle \sum_ {k \in \Gamma} \langle f, e _ {k} \rangle e _ {k}, g \Big \rangle \\ & = \sum_ {k \in \Gamma} \langle f, e _ {k} \rangle \langle e _ {k}, g \rangle \\ & = \sum_ {k \in \Gamma} \langle f, e _ {k} \rangle \overline {{\langle g , e _ {k} \rangle}}, \end{array}
$$

Equation (c) is called Parseval’s identity in honor of Marc-Antoine Parseval (1755–1836), who discovered a special case in 1799. 

where the first equation follows from (a) and the second equation follows from the definition of an unordered sum and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. 

Equation (c) follows from setting $g = f$ in (b). An alternative proof: equation (c) follows from 8.54(b) and the equation $f = \sum _ { k \in \Gamma } \langle f , e _ { k } \rangle e _ { k }$ from (a). 

## Gram–Schmidt Process and Existence of Orthonormal Bases

8.65 Example separable normed vector spaces 

Suppose $n \in { \mathbf { Z } } ^ { + }$ . Then $\mathbf { F } ^ { n }$ with the usual Hilbert space norm is separable because the closure of the countable set 

$$
\left\{\left(c _ {1}, \dots , c _ {n}\right) \in \mathbf {F} ^ {n}: \text { each } c _ {j} \text { is   rational } \right\}
$$

equals $\mathbf { F } ^ { n }$ (in case $\mathbf { F } = \mathbf { C } :$ to say that a complex number is rational in this context means that both the real and imaginary parts of the complex number are rational numbers in the usual sense). 

The Hilbert space $\ell ^ { 2 }$ is separable because the closure of the countable set 

$$
\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \left\{\left(c _ {1}, \dots , c _ {n}, 0, 0, \dots\right) \in \ell^ {2}: \text {   each   } c _ {j} \text {   is   rational   } \right\}
$$

is $\ell ^ { 2 }$ 

The Hilbert spaces $L ^ { 2 } ( [ 0 , 1 ] )$ and $L ^ { 2 } ( \mathbf { R } )$ are separable, as Exercise 13 asks you to verify [hint: consider finite linear combinations with rational coefficients of functions of the form $\chi _ { ( c , d ) } ,$ where c and d are rational numbers]. 

A moment’s thought about the definition of closure (see 6.7) shows that a normed vector space V is separable if and only if there exists a countable subset C of V such that every open ball in V contains at least one element of C. 

## 8.66 Example nonseparable normed vector spaces

Suppose Γ is an uncountable set. Then the Hilbert space $\ell ^ { 2 } ( \Gamma )$ is not separable. To see this, note that $\| \chi _ { \{ j \} } - \chi _ { \{ k \} } \| = \sqrt { 2 }$ for all $j , k \in \Gamma$ with $j \neq k$ . Hence 

$$
\left\{B \big (\chi_ {\{k \}}, \frac {\sqrt {2}}{2} \big): k \in \Gamma \right\}
$$

is an uncountable collection of disjoint open balls in $\ell ^ { 2 } ( \Gamma )$ ; no countable set can have at least one element in each of these balls. 

The Banach space $L ^ { \infty } ( [ 0 , 1 ] )$ is not separable. Here $\| \chi _ { [ 0 , s ] } - \chi _ { [ 0 , t ] } \| = 1$ for all $s , t \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ with $s \neq t$ . Thus 

$$
\left\{B \big (\chi_ {[ 0, t ]}, \frac {1}{2} \big): t \in [ 0, 1 ] \right\}
$$

is an uncountable collection of disjoint open balls in $L ^ { \infty } ( [ 0 , 1 ] )$ 

We present two proofs of the existence of orthonormal bases of Hilbert spaces. The first proof works only for separable Hilbert spaces, but it gives a useful algorithm, called the Gram–Schmidt process, for constructing orthonormal sequences. The second proof works for all Hilbert spaces, but it uses a result that depends upon the Axiom of Choice. 

Which proof should you read? In practice, the Hilbert spaces you will encounter will almost certainly be separable. Thus the first proof suffices, and it has the additional benefit of introducing you to a widely used algorithm. The second proof uses an entirely different approach and has the advantage of applying to separable and nonseparable Hilbert spaces. For maximum learning, read both proofs! 

8.67 existence of orthonormal bases for separable Hilbert spaces 

Every separable Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis. 

Proof Suppose V is a separable Hilbert space and $\left\{ f _ { 1 } , f _ { 2 } , \ldots \right\}$ is a countable subset of V whose closure equals V. We will inductively define an orthonormal sequence $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \mathbf { Z } ^ { + } }$ such that 

$$
\operatorname{span} \left\{f _ {1}, \dots , f _ {n} \right\} \subset \operatorname{span} \left\{e _ {1}, \dots , e _ {n} \right\}\tag{8.68}
$$

for each $n \in \mathbf { Z } ^ { + }$ . This will imply that ${ \overline { { \operatorname { s p a n } \{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \mathbf { Z } ^ { + } } } } } = V ,$ which will mean that $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in { \bf Z } ^ { + } }$ is an orthonormal basis of V. 

To get started with the induction, set $e _ { 1 } = f _ { 1 } / \| f _ { 1 } \|$ (we can assume that $f _ { 1 } \neq 0 )$ 

Now suppose $n \in \mathbf { Z } ^ { + }$ and $e _ { 1 } , \ldots , e _ { n }$ have been chosen so that $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \{ 1 , \dots , n \} }$ is an orthonormal family in V and 8.68 holds. If $f _ { k } \in \operatorname { s p a n } \{ e _ { 1 } , \ldots , e _ { n } \}$ for every $k \in \mathbf { Z } ^ { + }$ , then $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \{ 1 , \dots , n \} }$ is an orthonormal basis of V (completing the proof) and the process should be stopped. Otherwise, let m be the smallest positive integer such that 

8.69 

$$
f _ {m} \notin \operatorname{span} \left\{e _ {1}, \dots , e _ {n} \right\}.
$$

Define $e _ { n + 1 }$ by 

$$
e _ {n + 1} = \frac {f _ {m} - \langle f _ {m} , e _ {1} \rangle e _ {1} - \cdots - \langle f _ {m} , e _ {n} \rangle e _ {n}}{\| f _ {m} - \langle f _ {m} , e _ {1} \rangle e _ {1} - \cdots - \langle f _ {m} , e _ {n} \rangle e _ {n} \|}.\tag{8.70}
$$

Clearly $\| e _ { n + 1 } \| ~ = ~ 1$ (8.69 guarantees there is no division by 0). If $k \in \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ , then the equation above implies that $\left. e _ { n + 1 } , e _ { k } \right. \ = 0 .$ Thus $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \{ 1 , \dots , n + 1 \} }$ is an orthonormal family in V. Also, 8.68 and the choice of m as the smallest positive integer satisfying 8.69 imply that 

Jørgen Gram (1850–1916) and Erhard Schmidt (1876–1959) popularized this process that constructs orthonormal sequences. 

$$
\operatorname{span} \left\{f _ {1}, \dots , f _ {n + 1} \right\} \subset \operatorname{span} \left\{e _ {1}, \dots , e _ {n + 1} \right\},
$$

completing the induction and completing the proof. 

Before considering nonseparable Hilbert spaces, we take a short detour to illustrate how the Gram–Schmidt process used in the previous proof can be used to find closest elements to subspaces. We begin with a result connecting the orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace with an orthonormal basis of that subspace. 

## 8.71 orthogonal projection in terms of an orthonormal basis

Suppose that U is a closed subspace of a Hilbert space V and $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Gamma }$ is an orthonormal basis of U. Then 

$$
P _ {U} f = \sum_ {k \in \Gamma} \langle f, e _ {k} \rangle e _ {k}
$$

for all $f \in V .$ 

Proof Let $f \in V .$ If $k \in \Gamma$ , then 

$$
\langle f, e _ {k} \rangle = \langle f - P _ {U} f, e _ {k} \rangle + \langle P _ {U} f, e _ {k} \rangle = \langle P _ {U} f, e _ {k} \rangle ,
$$

where the last equality follows from 8.37(a). Now 

$$
P _ {U} f = \sum_ {k \in \Gamma} \langle P _ {U} f, e _ {k} \rangle e _ {k} = \sum_ {k \in \Gamma} \langle f, e _ {k} \rangle e _ {k},
$$

where the first equality follows from Parseval’s identity [8.63(a)] as applied to U and its orthonormal basis $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Gamma }$ , and the second equality follows from 8.72. 

## 8.73 Example best approximation

Find the polynomial g of degree at most 10 that minimizes 

$$
\int_ {- 1} ^ {1} \left| \sqrt {| x |} - g (x) \right| ^ {2} d x.
$$

Solution We will work in the real Hilbert space $L ^ { 2 } ( [ - 1 , 1 ] )$ with the usual inner product $\textstyle \langle g , h \rangle = \int _ { - 1 } ^ { 1 } g h$ . For $k \in \{ 0 , 1 , \ldots , 1 0 \}$ , let $f _ { k } \in L ^ { 2 } ( [ - 1 , 1 ] )$ be defined by $f _ { k } ( x ) = x ^ { k }$ . Let U be the subspace of $L ^ { 2 } ( [ - 1 , 1 ] )$ defined by 

$$
U = \operatorname{span} \left\{f _ {k} \right\} _ {k \in \{0, \dots , 1 0 \}}.
$$

Apply the Gram–Schmidt process from the proof of 8.67 to $\{ f _ { k } \} _ { k \in \{ 0 , . . . , 1 0 \} }$ , producing an orthonormal basis $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \{ 0 , \dots , 1 0 \} }$ of U, which is a closed subspace of $L ^ { 2 } ( [ - 1 , 1 ] )$ (see Exercise 8). The point here is that $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \{ 0 , . . . , 1 0 \} }$ can be computed explicitly and exactly by using 8.70 and evaluating some integrals (using software that can do exact rational arithmetic will make the process easier), getting $e _ { 0 } ( x ) = 1 / \sqrt { 2 }$ $e _ { 1 } ( x ) = \sqrt { 6 } x / 2 , . . .$ . up to 

$$
e _ {1 0} (x) = \frac {\sqrt {4 2}}{5 1 2} (- 6 3 + 3 4 6 5 x ^ {2} - 3 0 0 3 0 x ^ {4} + 9 0 0 9 0 x ^ {6} - 1 0 9 3 9 5 x ^ {8} + 4 6 1 8 9 x ^ {1 0}).
$$

Define $f \in L ^ { 2 } ( [ - 1 , 1 ] )$ by $f ( x ) \ = \ { \sqrt { | x | } }$ . Because U is the subspace of $L ^ { 2 } ( [ - 1 , 1 ] )$ consisting of polynomials of degree at most 10 and $P _ { U } f$ equals the element of U closest to $f$ (see 8.34), the formula in 8.71 tells us that the solution $g$ to our minimization problem is given by the formula 

$$
g = \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {1 0} \langle f, e _ {k} \rangle e _ {k}.
$$

Using the explicit expressions for $e _ { 0 } , \ldots , e _ { 1 0 }$ and again evaluating some integrals, this gives 

$$
g (x) = \frac {6 9 3 + 1 5 0 1 5 x ^ {2} - 6 4 3 5 0 x ^ {4} + 1 3 9 2 3 0 x ^ {6} - 1 3 8 5 6 7 x ^ {8} + 5 1 0 5 1 x ^ {1 0}}{2 9 4 4}.
$$

The figure here shows the graph of $f ( x ) = { \sqrt { | x | } }$ (red) and the graph of its closest polynomial $g$ (blue) of degree at most 10; here closest means as measured in the norm of $L ^ { 2 } ( [ - 1 , 1 ] )$ 

The approximation of $f$ by $g$ is pretty good, especially considering that f is not differentiable at 0 and thus a Taylor series expansion for $f$ does not make sense. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/dd468151-b8ed-4849-9b9d-66f1c76294ba/7ad02a4949f10f543757331014f8875b94fbda80d7196ff9e22b629536bc6dd5.jpg)


Recall that a subset Γ of a set V can be thought of as a family in V by considering $\{ e _ { f } \} _ { f \in \Gamma }$ , where $e _ { f } = f$ . With this convention, a subset Γ of an inner product space V is an orthonormal subset of V if $\| f \| = 1$ for all $f \in \Gamma$ and $\langle f , g \rangle = 0$ for all $f , g \in \Gamma$ with $f \neq g .$ 

The next result characterizes the orthonormal bases as the maximal elements among the collection of orthonormal subsets of a Hilbert space. Recall that a set $\Gamma \in { \mathcal { A } }$ in a collection of subsets of a set V is a maximal element of if there does not exist $\Gamma ^ { \prime } \in { \mathcal { A } }$ such that $\Gamma \subsetneq \Gamma ^ { \prime }$ (see 6.55). 

8.74 orthonormal bases as maximal elements
Suppose V is a Hilbert space, A is the collection of all orthonormal subsets of V, and $\Gamma$ is an orthonormal subset of V. Then $\Gamma$ is an orthonormal basis of V if and only if $\Gamma$ is a maximal element of A. 

Proof First suppose Γ is an orthonormal basis of V. Parseval’s identity [8.63(a)] implies that the only element of V that is orthogonal to every element of Γ is 0. Thus there does not exist an orthonormal subset of V that strictly contains Γ. In other words, Γ is a maximal element of ${ \mathcal { A } } .$ 

To prove the other direction, suppose now that Γ is a maximal element of ${ \mathcal { A } } .$ Let U denote the span of Γ. Then 

$$
U ^ {\perp} = \{0 \}
$$

because if f is a nonzero element of $U ^ { \perp }$ , then $\Gamma \cup \{ f / \| f \| \}$ is an orthonormal subset of V that strictly contains Γ. Hence U = V (by 8.42), which implies that Γ is an orthonormal basis of V. 

Now we are ready to prove that every Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis. Before reading the next proof, you may want to review the definition of a chain (6.58), which is a collection of sets such that for each pair of sets in the collection, one of them is contained in the other. You should also review $\mathrm { Z o r n } ^ { \prime } \mathrm { s }$ Lemma (6.60), which gives a way to show that a collection of sets contains a maximal element. 

Proof Suppose V is a Hilbert space. Let $\mathcal { A }$ be the collection of all orthonormal subsets of V. Suppose $\mathcal { C } \subset \mathcal { A }$ is a chain. Let L be the union of all the sets in . If $f \in L$ , then $\| f \| = 1$ because $f$ is an element of some orthonormal subset of V that is contained in $\mathcal { C }$ . 

If $f , g \in L$ with $f \neq g$ , then there exist orthonormal subsets Ω and Γ in $\mathcal { C }$ such that $f \in \Omega$ and $g \in \Gamma$ . Because $\mathcal { C }$ is a chain, either $\Omega \subset \Gamma$ or $\Gamma \subset \Omega$ . Either way, there is an orthonormal subset of $V$ that contains both $f$ and $g$ . Thus $\langle f , g \rangle = 0$ 

We have shown that L is an orthonormal subset of $V ;$ in other words, $L \in { \mathcal { A } }$ Thus Zorn’s Lemma (6.60) implies that $\mathcal { A }$ has a maximal element. Now 8.74 implies that V has an orthonormal basis. 

## Riesz Representation Theorem, Revisited

Now that we know that every Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis, we can give a completely different proof of the Riesz Representation Theorem (8.47) than the proof we gave earlier. 

Note that the new proof below of the Riesz Representation Theorem gives the formula 8.77 for h in terms of an orthonormal basis. One interesting feature of this formula is that h is uniquely determined by $\varphi$ and thus h does not depend upon the choice of an orthonormal basis. Hence despite its appearance, the right side of 8.77 is independent of the choice of an orthonormal basis. 

## 8.76 Riesz Representation Theorem

Suppose $\varphi$ is a bounded linear functional on a Hilbert space V and $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Gamma }$ is an orthonormal basis of $V .$ Let 

8.77 

$$
h = \sum_ {k \in \Gamma} \overline {{\varphi (e _ {k})}} e _ {k}.
$$

Then 

8.78 

$$
\varphi (f) = \langle f, h \rangle
$$

for all $f \in V .$ Furthermore, $\begin{array} { r } { \| \varphi \| = \left( \sum _ { k \in \Gamma } \vert \varphi ( e _ { k } ) \vert ^ { 2 } \right) ^ { 1 / 2 } } \end{array}$ 

Proof First we must show that the sum defining h makes sense. To do this, suppose Ω is a finite subset of Γ. Then 

$$
\sum_ {j \in \Omega} | \varphi (e _ {j}) | ^ {2} = \varphi \left(\sum_ {j \in \Omega} \overline {{\varphi (e _ {j})}} e _ {j}\right) \leq \| \varphi \| \left\| \sum_ {j \in \Omega} \overline {{\varphi (e _ {j})}} e _ {j} \right\| = \| \varphi \| \left(\sum_ {j \in \Omega} | \varphi (e _ {j}) | ^ {2}\right) ^ {1 / 2},
$$

where the last equality follows from 8.52. Dividing by $\left( \sum _ { j \in \Omega } \lvert \varphi ( e _ { j } ) \rvert ^ { 2 } \right) ^ { 1 / 2 }$ gives 

$$
\left(\sum_ {j \in \Omega} | \varphi (e _ {j}) | ^ {2}\right) ^ {1 / 2} \leq \| \varphi \|.
$$

Because the inequality above holds for every finite subset Ω of Γ, we conclude that 

$$
\sum_ {k \in \Gamma} | \varphi (e _ {k}) | ^ {2} \leq \| \varphi \| ^ {2}.
$$

Thus the sum defining h makes sense (by 8.54) in equation 8.77. 

Now 8.77 shows that $\langle h , e _ { j } \rangle = \varphi ( e _ { j } )$ for each $j \in \Gamma$ . Thus if $f \in V$ then 

$$
\varphi (f) = \varphi \left(\sum_ {k \in \Gamma} \langle f, e _ {k} \rangle e _ {k}\right) = \sum_ {k \in \Gamma} \langle f, e _ {k} \rangle \varphi (e _ {k}) = \sum_ {k \in \Gamma} \langle f, e _ {k} \rangle \overline {{\langle h , e _ {k} \rangle}} = \langle f, h \rangle ,
$$

where the first and last equalities follow from 8.63 and the second equality follows from the boundedness/continuity of $\varphi$ . Thus 8.78 holds. 

Finally, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, equation 8.78, and the equation $\varphi ( h ) =$ $\langle h , h \rangle$ show that $\begin{array} { r } { \| \varphi \| = \| h \| = \left( \sum _ { k \in \Gamma } \vert \varphi ( e _ { k } ) \vert ^ { 2 } \right) ^ { 1 / 2 } } \end{array}$

# Chapter 9 Real and Complex Measures

A measure is a countably additive function from a σ-algebra to $[ 0 , \infty ]$ . In this chapter, we consider countably additive functions from a σ-algebra to either R or C. The first section of this chapter shows that these functions, called real measures or complex measures, form an interesting Banach space with an appropriate norm. 

The second section of this chapter focuses on decomposition theorems that help us understand real and complex measures. These results will lead to a proof that the dual space of $L ^ { p } ( \mu )$ can be identified with $L ^ { p ^ { \prime } } ( \mu )$

## 9A Total Variation

## Properties of Real and Complex Measures

Recall that a measurable space is a pair $( X , S )$ , where $s$ is a σ-algebra on $X .$ Recall also that a measure on $( X , S )$ is a countably additive function from $s$ to $[ 0 , \infty ]$ that takes $\emptyset$ to 0. Countably additive functions that take values in R or C give us new objects called real measures or complex measures. 

9.1 Definition real and complex measures
Suppose $(X, \mathcal{S})$ is measurable space.
• A function $\nu: S \to F$ is called countably additive if $\nu\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty}E_{k}\right)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\nu(E_{k})$ for every disjoint sequence $E_{1}, E_{2}, \ldots$ of sets in S.
• A real measure on $(X, \mathcal{S})$ is a countably additive function $\nu: S \to R$ .
• A complex measure on $(X, \mathcal{S})$ is a countably additive function $\nu: S \to C$ . 

The word measure can be ambiguous in the mathematical literature. The most common use of the word measure is as we defined it in Chapter 2 (see 2.54). However, some mathematicians use the word measure to include what are here called real and complex measures; they then use the phrase positive measure to refer to what we defined as a measure in 

The terminology nonnegative measure would be more appropriate than positive measure because the function $\mu: \mathcal{S} \to \mathbf{F}$ defined by $\mu(E) = 0$ for every $E \in \mathcal{S}$ is a positive measure. However, we will stick with tradition and use the phrase positive measure. 

2.54. To help relieve this ambiguity, in this chapter we usually use the phrase (positive) measure to refer to measures as defined in 2.54. Putting positive in parentheses helps reinforce the idea that it is optional while distinguishing such measures from real and complex measures. 

9.2 Example real and complex measures 

Let λ denote Lebesgue measure on $[ - 1 , 1 ]$ . Define ν on the Borel subsets of $[ - 1 , 1 ]$ by 

$$
\nu (E) = \lambda \bigl (E \cap [ 0, 1 ] \bigr) - \lambda \bigl (E \cap [ - 1, 0) \bigr).
$$

Then ν is a real measure. 

$\operatorname { I f } \mu _ { 1 }$ and $\mu _ { 2 }$ are finite (positive) measures, then $\mu _ { 1 } - \mu _ { 2 }$ is a real measure and $\alpha _ { 1 } \mu _ { 1 } + \alpha _ { 2 } \mu _ { 2 }$ is a complex measure for all $\alpha _ { 1 } , \alpha _ { 2 } \in \mathbf { C } .$ 

If ν is a complex measure, then Re ν and Im ν are real measures. 

Note that every real measure is a complex measure. Note also that by definition, ∞ is not an allowable value for a real or complex measure. Thus a (positive) measure $\mu$ on $( X , S )$ is a real measure if and only if $\mu ( X ) < \infty$ 

Some authors use the terminology signed measure instead of real measure; some authors allow a real measure to take on the value ∞ or ∞ (but not both, because the expression ∞ ∞ must be avoided). However, real measures as defined here serve us better because we need to avoid ∞ when considering the Banach space of real or complex measures on a measurable space (see 9.18). 

For (positive) measures, we had to make $\mu ( \emptyset ) = 0$ part of the definition to avoid the function $\mu$ that assigns ∞ to all sets, including the empty set. But ∞ is not an allowable value for real or complex measures. Thus $\nu ( \emptyset ) = 0$ is a consequence of our definition rather than part of the definition, as shown in the next result. 

9.3 absolute convergence for a disjoint union
Suppose $\nu$ is a complex measure on a measurable space $(X, S)$ . Then
(a) $\nu(\emptyset) = 0;$ (b) $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}|\nu(E_k)| < \infty$ for every disjoint sequence $E_1, E_2, \ldots$ of sets in S. 

Proof To prove (a), note that $\varnothing , \varnothing , \ldots$ is a disjoint sequence of sets in $s$ whose union equals $\emptyset$ . Thus 

$$
\nu (\emptyset) = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \nu (\emptyset).
$$

The right side of the equation above makes sense as an element of R or C only when $\nu ( \emptyset ) = 0$ , which proves (a). 

To prove (b), suppose $E _ { 1 } , E _ { 2 } , \dots$ is a disjoint sequence of sets in $s$ . First suppose ν is a real measure. Thus 

$$
\nu \Big (\bigcup_ {\{k: \nu (E _ {k}) > 0 \}} E _ {k} \Big) = \sum_ {\{k: \nu (E _ {k}) > 0 \}} \nu (E _ {k}) = \sum_ {\{k: \nu (E _ {k}) > 0 \}} | \nu (E _ {k}) |
$$

and 

$$
- \nu \left(\bigcup_ {\{k: \nu (E _ {k}) <   0 \}} E _ {k}\right) = - \sum_ {\{k: \nu (E _ {k}) <   0 \}} \nu (E _ {k}) = \sum_ {\{k: \nu (E _ {k}) <   0 \}} | \nu (E _ {k}) |.
$$

Because $\nu ( E ) \in \mathbf { R }$ for every $E \in { \mathcal { S } }$ , the right side of the last two displayed equations is finite. Thus $\textstyle \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { \infty } \vert \nu ( E _ { k } ) \vert < \infty$ , as desired. 

Now consider the case where ν is a complex measure. Then 

$$
\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} | \nu (E _ {k}) | \leq \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \left(| (\operatorname{Re} \nu) (E _ {k}) | + | (\operatorname{Im} \nu) (E _ {k}) |\right) <   \infty ,
$$

where the last inequality follows from applying the result for real measures to the real measures Re ν and Im ν. 

The next definition provides an important class of examples of real and complex measures. 

## 9.4 measure determined by an $\mathcal { L } ^ { 1 }$ -function

Suppose $\mu$ is a (positive) measure on a measurable space $( X , S )$ and $h \in \mathcal { L } ^ { 1 } ( \mu )$ Define ν : $\mathcal { S }  \mathbf { F }$ by 

$$
\nu (E) = \int_ {E} h d \mu .
$$

Then ν is a real measure on (X, ) if F = R and is a complex measure on $( X , S )$ if $\mathbf { F } = \mathbf { C } .$ 

Proof Suppose $E _ { 1 } , E _ { 2 } , \dots$ is a disjoint sequence of sets in $s$ . Then 

$$
\nu \Bigl (\bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {k} \Bigr) = \int \Bigl (\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \chi_ {E _ {k}} (x) h (x) \Bigr) d \mu (x) = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \int \chi_ {E _ {k}} h d \mu = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \nu (E _ {k}),\tag{9.5}
$$

where the first equality holds because the sets $E _ { 1 } , E _ { 2 } , \dots$ . are disjoint and the second equality follows from the inequality 

$$
\Big | \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {m} \chi_ {E _ {k}} (x) h (x) \Big | \leq | h (x) |,
$$

which along with the assumption that $h \in \mathcal { L } ^ { 1 } ( \mu )$ allows us to interchange the integral and limit of the partial sums by the Dominated Convergence Theorem (3.31). 

The countable additivity shown in 9.5 means ν is a real or complex measure. 

The next definition simply gives a notation for the measure defined in the previous result. In the notation that we are about to define, the symbol d has no separate meaning—it functions to separate h and $\mu$ 

## 9.6 Definition h dµ

Suppose $\mu$ is a (positive) measure on a measurable space $( X , S )$ and $h \in \mathcal { L } ^ { 1 } ( \mu )$ Then h dµ is the real or complex measure on $( X , S )$ defined by 

$$
(h d \mu) (E) = \int_ {E} h d \mu .
$$

Note that if a function $h \in \mathcal { L } ^ { 1 } ( \mu )$ takes values in $[ 0 , \infty )$ , then h dµ is a finite (positive) measure. 

The next result shows some basic properties of complex measures. No proofs are given because the proofs are the same as the proofs of the corresponding results for (positive) measures. Specifically, see the proofs of 2.57, 2.61, 2.59, and 2.60. Because complex measures cannot take on the value ∞, we do not need to worry about hypotheses of finite measure that are required of the (positive) measure versions of all but part (c). 

Suppose $\nu$ is a real measure on a measurable space $(X, \mathcal{S})$ and $E \in \mathcal{S}$ . Then $|\nu|(E) = \sup \{|\nu(A)| + |\nu(B)| : A, B$ are disjoint sets in $\mathcal{S}$ and $A \cup B \subset E\}$ . 

9.8 Definition total variation measure
Suppose $\nu$ is a complex measure on a measurable space $(X, S)$ . The total variation measure is the function $|\nu|: S \to [0, \infty]$ defined by $|\nu|(E) = \sup\{|\nu(E_1)| + \cdots + |\nu(E_n)| : n \in \mathbf{Z}^+ \text{ and } E_1, \ldots, E_n$ are disjoint sets in S such that $E_1 \cup \cdots \cup E_n \subset E$ . 

## 9.7 properties of complex measures

Suppose $\nu$ is a complex measure on a measurable space $(X, S)$ . Then
(a) $\nu(E \setminus D) = \nu(E) - \nu(D)$ for all $D, E \in S$ with $D \subset E$ ;
(b) $\nu(D \cup E) = \nu(D) + \nu(E) - \nu(D \cap E)$ for all $D, E \in S$ ;
(c) $\nu\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty}E_{k}\right)=\lim_{k\to\infty}\nu(E_{k})$ for all increasing sequences $E_{1} \subset E_{2} \subset \cdots$ of sets in S;
(d) $\nu\left(\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty}E_{k}\right)=\lim_{k\to\infty}\nu(E_{k})$ for all decreasing sequences $E_{1} \supset E_{2} \supset \cdots$ of sets in S. 

## Total Variation Measure

We use the terminology total variation measure below even though we have not yet shown that the object being defined is a measure. Soon we will justify this terminology (see 9.11). 

To start getting familiar with the definition above, you should verify that if ν is a complex measure on $( X , S )$ and $E \in { \mathcal { S } }$ , then 

$| \nu ( E ) | \leq | \nu | ( E )$ 

$| \nu | ( E ) = \nu ( E )$ if ν is a finite (positive) measure; 

$| \nu | ( E ) = 0 { \mathrm { i f } }$ and only if $\nu ( A ) = 0$ for every $A \in S$ such that $A \subset E$ 

The next result states that for real measures, we can consider only $n = 2$ in the definition of the total variation measure. 

## 9.9 total variation measure of a real measure

Proof Suppose that $n \in { \bf Z } ^ { + }$ and $E _ { 1 } , \ldots , E _ { n }$ are disjoint sets in $s$ such that $E _ { 1 } \cup \cdots \cup E _ { n } \subset E$ . Let 

$$
A = \bigcup_ {\{k: \nu (E _ {k}) > 0 \}} E _ {k} \quad \text { and } \quad B = \bigcup_ {\{k: \nu (E _ {k}) <   0 \}} E _ {k}.
$$

Then $A , B$ are disjoint sets in $s$ and $A \cup B \subset E$ . Furthermore, 

$$
| \nu (A) | + | \nu (B) | = | \nu (E _ {1}) | + \dots + | \nu (E _ {n}) |.
$$

Thus in the supremum that defines $| \nu | ( E )$ , we can take $n = 2$ 

The next result could be rephrased as stating that if $h \in \mathcal { L } ^ { 1 } ( \mu )$ , then the total variation measure of the measure h dµ is the measure $| h | d \mu$ . In the statement below, the notation $d \nu = h d \mu$ means the same as $\nu = h d \mu ;$ the notation dν is commonly used when considering expressions involving measures of the form h dµ. 

9.10 total variation measure of $h \, d\mu$ Suppose $\mu$ is a (positive) measure on a measurable space $(X, \mathcal{S})$ , $h \in \mathcal{L}^{1}(\mu)$ , and $dv = h \, d\mu$ . Then $|\nu|(E) = \int_{E} |h| \, d\mu$ for every $E \in S$ . 

Proof Suppose that $E \in S$ . If $E _ { 1 } , \ldots , E _ { n }$ is a disjoint sequence in $s$ such that $E _ { 1 } \cup \cdots \cup E _ { n } \subset E$ , then 

$$
\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} | \nu (E _ {k}) | = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} \left| \int_ {E _ {k}} h d \mu \right| \leq \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} \int_ {E _ {k}} | h | d \mu \leq \int_ {E} | h | d \mu .
$$

The inequality above implies that $\textstyle | \nu | ( E ) \leq \int _ { E } | h | d \mu$ 

To prove the inequality in the other direction, first suppose $\mathbf { F } = \mathbf { R }$ ; thus h is a real-valued function and ν is a real measure. Let 

$$
A = \{x \in E: h (x) > 0 \} \quad \text { and } \quad B = \{x \in E: h (x) <   0 \}.
$$

Then A and B are disjoint sets in and $A \cup B \subset E$ . We have 

$$
| \nu (A) | + | \nu (B) | = \int_ {A} h d \mu - \int_ {B} h d \mu = \int_ {E} | h | d \mu .
$$

Thus $| \nu | ( E ) \geq \int _ { E } | h |$ dµ, completing the proof in the case $\mathbf { F } = \mathbf { R }$ 

Now suppose ${ \bf { \bar { F } } } = { \bf { C } } ;$ ; thus ν is a complex measure. Let $\varepsilon > 0$ . There exists a simple function $g \in \mathcal { L } ^ { 1 } ( \mu )$ such that $\| g - h \| _ { 1 } < \varepsilon ( { \bf b y } 3 . 4 4 )$ . There exist disjoint sets $E _ { 1 } , \dots , E _ { n } \in { \mathcal { S } }$ and $c _ { 1 } , \ldots , c _ { n } \in \mathbf { C }$ such that $E _ { 1 } \cup \cdots \cup E _ { n } \subset E$ and 

$$
g | _ {E} = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} c _ {k} \chi_ {E _ {k}}.
$$

Now 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} | \nu (E _ {k}) | = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} \Big | \int_ {E _ {k}} h d \mu \Big | \\ \qquad \qquad \geq \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} \Big | \int_ {E _ {k}} g d \mu \Big | - \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} \Big | \int_ {E _ {k}} (g - h) d \mu \Big | \\ \qquad \qquad = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} | c _ {k} | \mu (E _ {k}) - \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} \Big | \int_ {E _ {k}} (g - h) d \mu \Big | \\ \qquad \qquad = \int_ {E} | g | d \mu - \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} \Big | \int_ {E _ {k}} (g - h) d \mu \Big | \\ \qquad \qquad \geq \int_ {E} | g | d \mu - \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} \int_ {E _ {k}} | g - h | d \mu \\ \qquad \qquad \geq \int_ {E} | h | d \mu - 2 \varepsilon . \end{array}
$$

The inequality above implies that $\textstyle | \nu | ( E ) \geq \int _ { E } | h | d \mu - 2 \varepsilon$ . Because $\varepsilon$ is an arbitrary positive number, this implies $\begin{array} { r } { | \nu | ( E ) \geq \int _ { E } | h | ^ { \prime } d \mu } \end{array}$ , completing the proof. 

Now we justify the terminology total variation measure. 

9.11 total variation measure is a measure
Suppose $\nu$ is a complex measure on a measurable space $(X, \mathcal{S})$ . Then the total variation function $|\nu|$ is a (positive) measure on $(X, \mathcal{S})$ .
Proof The definition of $|\nu|$ and 9.3(a) imply that $|\nu| (\emptyset) = 0$ .
To show that $|\nu|$ is countably additive, suppose $A_1, A_2, \ldots$ are disjoint sets in $\mathcal{S}$ . Fix $m \in \mathbf{Z}^+$ . For each $k \in \{1, \ldots, m\}$ , suppose $E_{1,k}, \ldots, E_{n_k,k}$ are disjoint sets in $\mathcal{S}$ such that
9.12 $E_{1,k} \cup \ldots \cup E_{n_k,k} \subset A_k$ .
Then $\{E_{j,k}: 1 \leq k \leq m$ and $1 \leq j \leq n_k\}$ is a disjoint collection of sets in $\mathcal{S}$ that are all contained in $\bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} A_k$ . Hence $\sum_{k=1}^{m} \sum_{j=1}^{n_k} |\nu(E_{j,k})| \leq |\nu| \left( \bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} A_k \right)$ .
Taking the supremum of the left side of the inequality above over all choices of $\{E_{j,k}\}$ satisfying 9.12 shows that $\sum_{k=1}^{m} |\nu|(A_k) \leq |\nu| \left( \bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} A_k \right)$ .
Because the inequality above holds for all $m \in \mathbf{Z}^+$ , we have $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} |\nu|(A_k) \leq |\nu| \left( \bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} A_k \right)$ . 

To prove the inequality above in the other direction, suppose $E _ { 1 } , \dots , E _ { n } \in { \mathcal { S } }$ are disjoint sets such that $E _ { 1 } \cup \cdot \cdot \cdot \cup E _ { n } \subset \bigcup _ { k = 1 } ^ { \infty } A _ { k }$ . Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} | \nu | (A _ {k}) \geq \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} | \nu (E _ {j} \cap A _ {k}) | \\ \qquad = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} | \nu (E _ {j} \cap A _ {k}) | \\ \qquad \geq \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \Big | \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \nu (E _ {j} \cap A _ {k}) \Big | \\ \qquad = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} | \nu (E _ {j}) |, \end{array}
$$

where the first line above follows from the definition of $| \nu | ( A _ { k } )$ and the last line above follows from the countable additivity of ν. 

The inequality above and the definition of $| \nu | \left( \bigcup _ { k = 1 } ^ { \infty } A _ { k } \right)$ imply that 

$$
\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} | \nu | (A _ {k}) \geq | \nu | \Bigl (\bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} A _ {k} \Bigr),
$$

completing the proof. 

## The Banach Space of Measures

In this subsection, we make the set of complex or real measures on a measurable space into a vector space and then into a Banach space. 

9.13 Definition addition and scalar multiplication of measures
Suppose $(X, \mathcal{S})$ is a measurable space. For complex measures $\nu, \mu$ on $(X, \mathcal{S})$ and $\alpha \in F$ , define complex measures $\nu + \mu$ and $\alpha\nu$ on $(X, \mathcal{S})$ by $(\nu + \mu)(E) = \nu(E) + \mu(E)$ and $(\alpha\nu)(E) = \alpha(\nu(E))$ . 

You should verify that if $\nu , \mu ,$ , and α are as above, then $\nu + \mu$ and αν are complex measures on $( X , S )$ . You should also verify that these natural definitions of addition and scalar multiplication make the set of complex (or real) measures on a measurable space $( X , S )$ into a vector space. We now introduce notation for this vector space. 

9.14 Definition $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{F}}(\mathcal{S})$ Suppose $(X, \mathcal{S})$ is a measurable space. Then $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{F}}(\mathcal{S})$ denotes the vector space of real measures on $(X, \mathcal{S})$ if F = R and denotes the vector space of complex measures on $(X, \mathcal{S})$ if F = C. 

We use the terminology total variation norm below even though we have not yet shown that the object being defined is a norm (especially because it is not obvious that $\| \nu \| <$ ∞ for every complex measure ν). Soon we will justify this terminology. 

<table><tr><td>9.15 Definition total variation norm of a complex measure</td></tr><tr><td>Suppose <eq>\nu</eq> is a complex measure on a measurable space <eq>(X, S)</eq>. The total variation norm of <eq>\nu</eq>, denoted <eq>||\nu||</eq>, is defined by<eq>||\nu|| = | \nu |(X)</eq>.</td></tr></table>

## 9.16 Example total variation norm

$\operatorname { I f } \mu$ is a finite (positive) measure, then $\| \mu \| = \mu ( X )$ , as you should verify. 

If $\mu$ is a (positive) measure, $h \in \mathcal { L } ^ { 1 } ( \mu )$ , and $\ a \nu = h d \mu$ , then $\lVert \nu \rVert = \lVert h \rVert _ { 1 }$ (as follows from 9.10). 

The next result implies that if ν is a complex measure on a measurable space $( X , S )$ , then $| \nu | ( E ) <$ ∞ for every $E \in { \mathcal { S } }$ 

<table><tr><td>9.17 total variation norm is finite</td></tr><tr><td>Suppose (X, S) is a measurable space and <eq>\nu \in \mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{F}}(\mathcal{S})</eq>. Then <eq>\| \nu \| &lt; \infty</eq>.</td></tr></table>

Proof First consider the case where $\mathbf { F } = \mathbf { R }$ . Thus ν is a real measure on $( X , S )$ . To begin this proof by contradiction, suppose $\| \nu \| = | \nu | ( X ) = \infty$ 

We inductively choose a decreasing sequence $E _ { 0 } \supset E _ { 1 } \supset E _ { 2 } \supset \cdots$ of sets in $s$ as follows: Start by choosing $E _ { 0 } = X$ . Now suppose $n \geq 0$ and $E _ { n } \in { \mathcal { S } }$ has been chosen with $| \nu | ( E _ { n } ) = \infty$ and $| \nu ( E _ { n } ) | \geq n$ . Because $| \nu | ( E _ { n } ) = \infty ,$ 9.9 implies that there exists $A \in S$ such that $A \subset E _ { n }$ and $| \nu ( A ) | \geq n + 1 + | \nu ( E _ { n } ) |$ , which implies that 

$$
| \nu (E _ {n} \setminus A) | = | \nu (E _ {n}) - \nu (A) | \geq | \nu (A) | - | \nu (E _ {n}) | \geq n + 1.
$$

Now 

$$
| \nu | (A) + | \nu | (E _ {n} \setminus A) = | \nu | (E _ {n}) = \infty
$$

because the total variation measure $| \nu |$ is a (positive) measure (by 9.11). The equation above shows that at least one of $| \nu | ( A )$ and $\left| \nu \right| \left( E _ { n } \setminus A \right)$ is ∞. Let $E _ { n + 1 } = A$ if $| \nu | ( A ) = \infty$ and let $E _ { n + 1 } ~ = ~ E _ { n } \setminus A$ if $| \nu | ( A ) < \infty$ . Thus $E _ { n } ~ \supset ~ E _ { n + 1 }$ $| \nu | ( E _ { n + 1 } ) = \infty$ , and $| \nu ( E _ { n + 1 } ) | \geq n + 1$ 

Now $9 . 7 ( \mathrm { d } )$ implies that $\begin{array} { r } { \nu \left( \bigcap _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n } \right) = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } \nu ( E _ { n } ) } \end{array}$ . However, $| \nu ( E _ { n } ) | \geq n$ for each $n \in { \mathbf { Z } } ^ { + }$ , and thus the limit in the last equation does not exist (in R). This contradiction completes the proof in the case where ν is a real measure. 

Consider now the case where $\mathbf { F } = \mathbf { C } $ ; thus ν is a complex measure on $( X , S )$ Then 

$$
| \nu | (X) \leq | \operatorname{Re} \nu | (X) + | \operatorname{Im} \nu | (X) <   \infty ,
$$

where the last inequality follows from applying the real case to Re ν and Im ν. 

The previous result tells us that if $( X , S )$ is a measurable space, then $\| \nu \| <$ ∞ for all $\nu \in \mathcal { M } _ { \mathrm { F } } ( S )$ . This implies (as the reader should verify) that the total variation norm $\left\| \cdot \right\|$ is a norm on $\mathcal { M } _ { \mathbf { F } } ( \cal { S } )$ . The next result shows that this norm makes $\mathcal { M } _ { \bf F } ( S )$ into a Banach space (in other words, every Cauchy sequence in this norm converges). 

<table><tr><td>9.18 the set of real or complex measures on (X, S) is a Banach space</td></tr><tr><td>Suppose (X, S) is a measurable space. Then <eq>\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{F}}(\mathcal{S})</eq> is a Banach space with the total variation norm.</td></tr></table>

Proof Suppose $\nu _ { 1 } , \nu _ { 2 } , \ldots$ is a Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal { M } _ { \mathbf { F } } ( \cal { S } )$ . For each $E \in S$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} | \nu_ {j} (E) - \nu_ {k} (E) | & = | (\nu_ {j} - \nu_ {k}) (E) | \\ & \leq | \nu_ {j} - \nu_ {k} | (E) \\ & \leq \| \nu_ {j} - \nu_ {k} \|. \end{array}
$$

Thus $\nu _ { 1 } ( E ) , \nu _ { 2 } ( E ) , . . .$ . is a Cauchy sequence in F and hence converges. Thus we can define a function $\nu \colon S  \mathbf { F }$ by 

$$
\nu (E) = \lim _ {j \to \infty} \nu_ {j} (E).
$$

To show that $\nu \in \mathcal { M } _ { \mathrm { F } } ( S )$ , we must verify that ν is countably additive. To do this, suppose $E _ { 1 } , E _ { 2 } , \dots$ is a disjoint sequence of sets in ${ \mathcal { S } } .$ . Let $\varepsilon > 0$ . Let $m \in { \mathbf Z } ^ { + }$ be such that 

9.19 

$$
\left\| \nu_ {j} - \nu_ {k} \right\| \leq \varepsilon \quad \text { for   all } j, k \geq m.
$$

If $n \in \mathbf { Z } ^ { + }$ is such that 

$$
\sum_ {k = n} ^ {\infty} | \nu_ {m} (E _ {k}) | \leq \varepsilon\tag{9.20}
$$

[such an n exists by applying 9.3(b) to $\nu _ { m } ]$ and if $j \geq m$ , then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {k = n} ^ {\infty} | \nu_ {j} (E _ {k}) | \leq \sum_ {k = n} ^ {\infty} | (\nu_ {j} - \nu_ {m}) (E _ {k}) | + \sum_ {k = n} ^ {\infty} | \nu_ {m} (E _ {k}) | \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \sum_ {k = n} ^ {\infty} | \nu_ {j} - \nu_ {m} | (E _ {k}) + \varepsilon \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad = | \nu_ {j} - \nu_ {m} | \Big (\bigcup_ {k = n} ^ {\infty} E _ {k} \Big) + \varepsilon \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq 2 \varepsilon , \end{array}\tag{9.21}
$$

where the second line uses 9.20, the third line uses the countable additivity of the measure $| \nu _ { j } - \nu _ { m } |$ (see 9.11), and the fourth line uses 9.19. 

If ε and n are as in the paragraph above, then 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \Big | \nu \Big (\bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {k} \Big) - \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n - 1} \nu (E _ {k}) \Big | = \Big | \lim _ {j \to \infty} \nu_ {j} \Big (\bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {k} \Big) - \lim _ {j \to \infty} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n - 1} \nu_ {j} (E _ {k}) \Big | \\ = \lim _ {j \to \infty} \Big | \sum_ {k = n} ^ {\infty} \nu_ {j} (E _ {k}) \Big | \\ \leq 2 \varepsilon , \end{array}
$$

where the second line uses the countable additivity of the measure $\nu _ { j }$ and the third line uses 9.21. The inequality above implies that $\nu \big ( \mathsf { U } _ { k = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { k } \big ) = \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { \infty } \dot { \nu } \big ( E _ { k } \big )$ , completing the proof that $\nu \in \mathcal { M } _ { \mathrm { F } } ( S )$ 

We still need to prove that lim $\lvert \ j _ { k } \to \infty  \| \nu - \nu _ { k } \| = 0$ . To do this, suppose $\varepsilon > 0$ . Let $m \in { \mathbf Z } ^ { + }$ be such that 

$$
\left\| \nu_ {j} - \nu_ {k} \right\| \leq \varepsilon \quad \text { for   all } j, k \geq m.\tag{9.22}
$$

Suppose $k \geq m$ . Suppose also that $E _ { 1 } , \dots , E _ { n } \in { \mathcal { S } }$ are disjoint subsets of $X .$ . Then 

$$
\sum_ {\ell = 1} ^ {n} | (\nu - \nu_ {k}) (E _ {\ell}) | = \lim _ {j \to \infty} \sum_ {\ell = 1} ^ {n} | (\nu_ {j} - \nu_ {k}) (E _ {\ell}) | \leq \varepsilon ,
$$

where the last inequality follows from 9.22 and the definition of the total variation norm. The inequality above implies that $\left\| \nu - \nu _ { k } \right\| \leq \varepsilon .$ , completing the proof.

\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} | \nu (E _ {k}) | <   t.
$$

[This exercise shows that the supremum in the definition of $| \nu | ( [ 0 , t ] )$ is not attained, even ifcountably many disjoint sets are allowed.]

In other words, show that there does not exist an inner product $\langle \cdot , \cdot \rangle$ on $\mathcal { M } _ { \bf F } ( S )$ such that $\lVert \nu \rVert = \langle \nu , \nu \rangle ^ { 1 / 2 }$ for all $\nu \in \mathcal { M } _ { \mathrm { F } } ( S )$ , where $\left\| \cdot \right\|$ is the usual total variation norm on $\mathcal { M } _ { \mathbf { F } } ( \cal { S } )$ 

11 For $( X , S )$ a measurable space and $b \in X$ , define a finite (positive) measure $\delta _ { b }$ on $( X , S )$ by

\delta_ {b} (E) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & \text { if } b \in E, \\ 0 & \text { if } b \notin E \end{array} \right.
