# 10D Spectral Theorem for Compact Operators

## Orthonormal Bases Consisting of Eigenvectors

We begin this section with the following useful lemma. 

<table><tr><td>10.96 <eq>T^{*}T - \|T\|^{2}I</eq> is not invertible</td></tr><tr><td>If <eq>T</eq> is a bounded operator on a nonzero Hilbert space, then <eq>\|T\|^{2} \in \text{sp}(T^{*}T)</eq>.</td></tr></table>

Proof Suppose T is a bounded operator on a nonzero Hilbert space V. Let $f _ { 1 } , f _ { 2 } , \ldots$ be a sequence in V such that $\| f _ { n } \| = 1$ for each $n \in \mathbf { Z } ^ { + }$ and 

10.97 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \| T f _ {n} \| = \| T \|.
$$

Then 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\left| \left| T ^ {*} T f _ {n} - \| T \| ^ {2} f _ {n} \right| \right| ^ {2} = \| T ^ {*} T f _ {n} \| ^ {2} - 2 \| T \| ^ {2} \langle T ^ {*} T f _ {n}, f _ {n} \rangle + \| T \| ^ {4}} \\ & {\qquad = \| T ^ {*} T f _ {n} \| ^ {2} - 2 \| T \| ^ {2} \| T f _ {n} \| ^ {2} + \| T \| ^ {4}} \\ & {\qquad \leq 2 \| T \| ^ {4} - 2 \| T \| ^ {2} \| T f _ {n} \| ^ {2},} \end{array}
$$

10.98 

where the last line holds because $\| T ^ { * } T f _ { n } \| \leq \| T ^ { * } \| \| T f _ { n } \| \leq \| T \| ^ { 2 }$ . Now 10.97 and 10.98 imply that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} (T ^ {*} T - \| T \| ^ {2} I) f _ {n} = 0.
$$

Because $\| f _ { n } \| = 1$ for each $n \in \mathbf { Z } ^ { + }$ , the equation above implies that $T ^ { * } T - \| T \| ^ { 2 } I$ is not invertible, as desired. 

The next result indicates one way in which self-adjoint compact operators behave like self-adjoint operators on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. 

<table><tr><td>10.99 every self-adjoint compact operator has an eigenvalue.</td></tr><tr><td>Suppose T is a self-adjoint compact operator on a nonzero Hilbert space. Then either ||T|| or -||T|| is an eigenvalue of T.</td></tr></table>

Proof Because T is self-adjoint, 10.96 states that $T ^ { 2 } - \| T \| ^ { 2 } I$ is not invertible. Now 

$$
T ^ {2} - \| T \| ^ {2} I = (T - \| T \| I) (T + \| T \| I).
$$

Thus $T - \| T \| I$ and $T + \lVert T \rVert I$ cannot both be invertible. Hence $\| T \| \in \mathsf { s p } ( T )$ or $- \| T \| \in \mathsf { s p } ( T )$ . Because T is compact, 10.85 now implies that $\| T \| \ \mathrm { o r } - \| \bar { T } \|$ is an eigenvalue of T, as desired, or that $\| T \| = 0$ , which means that $T = 0$ , in which case 0 is an eigenvalue of T. 

```txt
10.101 Example invariant subspaces 
```

If $T$ is a compact operator on a Hilbert space and $U$ is an invariant subspace for $T$ , then $T|_{U}$ is a compact operator on $U$ , as follows from the definitions. If $U$ is an invariant subspace for a self-adjoint operator $T$ , then $T|_{U}$ is self-adjoint because The most important open question in operator theory is the invariant subspace problem, which asks whether every bounded operator on a Hilbert space with dimension greater than 1 has a closed invariant subspace other than $\{0\}$ and $V$ . 

If T is an operator on a vector space V and U is a subspace of $V ,$ then $T | _ { U }$ is a linear map from U to V. For $T | _ { U }$ to be an operator (meaning that it is a linear map from a vector space to itself), we need $T ( U ) \subset U$ . Thus we are led to the following definition. 

10.100 Definition invariant subspace
Suppose T is an operator on a vector space V. A subspace U of V is called an invariant subspace for T if $Tf \in U$ for every $f \in U$ . 

You should verify each of the assertions below. 

For $b \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ , the subspace 

$$
\{f \in L ^ {2} ([ 0, 1 ]): f (t) = 0
$$

$$
t \in [ 0, b ] \}
$$

is an invariant subspace for the Volterra operator $\mathcal{V}\colon L^{2}([0,1])\to L^{2}([0,1])$ defined by $(\mathcal{V}f)(x) = \int_0^x f.$ 

Suppose T is an operator on a Hilbert space V and $f \in V$ with $f \neq 0$ . Then span f  is an invariant subspace for T if and only if f is an eigenvector of T. 

Suppose T is an operator on a Hilbert space V. Then 0 , V, null T, and range T are invariant subspaces for T. 

If T is a bounded operator on a Hilbert space and U is an invariant subspace for T, then U is an invariant subspace for T. 

$$
\langle (T | _ {U}) f, g \rangle = \langle T f, g \rangle = \langle f, T g \rangle = \langle f, (T | _ {U}) g \rangle
$$

for all $f , g \in U$ . The next result shows that a bit more is true. 

10.102 U invariant for self-adjoint T implies $U^{\perp}$ invariant for T

Suppose U is an invariant subspace for a self-adjoint operator T. Then
(a) $U^{\perp}$ is also an invariant subspace for T;
(b) $T|_{U^{\perp}}$ is a self-adjoint operator on $U^{\perp}$ . 

Proof To prove (a), suppose $f \in U ^ { \perp } . \operatorname { I f } g \in U .$ , then 

$$
\langle T f, g \rangle = \langle f, T g \rangle = 0,
$$

where the first equality holds because T is self-adjoint and the second equality holds because $T g \in U$ and $f \in U ^ { \perp }$ . Because the equation above holds for all $g \in U$ , we conclude that $T f \in \dot { U } ^ { \perp }$ . Thus $U ^ { \perp }$ is an invariant subspace for $T ,$ proving (a). 

By part (a), we can think of $T | _ { U ^ { \rfloor } }$ as an operator on $U ^ { \perp }$ . To prove (b), suppose $h \in U ^ { \perp } . \operatorname { I f } f \in U ^ { \perp }$ , then 

$$
\langle f, (T | _ {U ^ {\perp}}) ^ {*} h \rangle = \langle T | _ {U ^ {\perp}} f, h \rangle = \langle T f, h \rangle = \langle f, T h \rangle = \langle f, T | _ {U ^ {\perp}} h \rangle .
$$

Because $( T | _ { U ^ { \perp } } ) ^ { * } h$ and $T | _ { U ^ { \rfloor } }$ h are both in $U ^ { \perp }$ and the equation above holds for all $f \in U ^ { \perp }$ , we conclude that $( T | _ { U ^ { \bot } } ) ^ { * } h = T | _ { U ^ { \bot } } h$ , proving (b). 

Operators for which there exists an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors may be the easiest operators to understand. The next result states that any such operator must be self-adjoint in the case of a real Hilbert space and normal in the case of a complex Hilbert space. 

```txt
10.103 orthonormal basis of eigenvectors implies self-adjoint or normal
Suppose T is a bounded operator on a Hilbert space V and there is an orthonormal basis of V consisting of eigenvectors of T.
(a) If F = R, then T is self-adjoint.
(b) If F = C, then T is normal. 
```

Proof Suppose $\{ e _ { j } \} _ { j \in \Gamma }$ is an orthonormal basis of V such that $e _ { j }$ is an eigenvector of T for each $j \in \Gamma$ . Thus there exists a family $\{ \alpha _ { j } \} _ { j \in \Gamma }$ in F such that 

10.104 

$$
T e _ {j} = \alpha_ {j} e _ {j}
$$

for each $j \in \Gamma$ . If $k \in \Gamma$ and $f \in V ,$ then 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \langle f, T ^ {*} e _ {k} \rangle = \langle T f, e _ {k} \rangle = \Big \langle T \Big (\sum_ {j \in \Gamma} \langle f, e _ {j} \rangle e _ {j} \Big), e _ {k} \Big \rangle \\ = \Big \langle \sum_ {j \in \Gamma} \alpha_ {j} \langle f, e _ {j} \rangle e _ {j}, e _ {k} \Big \rangle = \alpha_ {k} \langle f, e _ {k} \rangle = \langle f, \overline {{\alpha_ {k}}} e _ {k} \rangle . \end{array}
$$

The equation above implies that 

10.105 

$$
T ^ {*} e _ {k} = \overline {{\alpha_ {k}}} e _ {k}.
$$

To prove (a), suppose $\mathbf { F } = \mathbf { R }$ . Then 10.105 and 10.104 imply $T ^ { * } e _ { k } = \alpha _ { k } e _ { k } = T e _ { k }$ for each $k \in K$ . Hence $T ^ { * } = T$ , completing the proof of (a). 

To prove (b), now suppose $\mathbf { F } = \mathbf { C } . \mathrm { I f } \ k \in \Gamma$ , then 10.105 and 10.104 imply that 

$$
(T ^ {*} T) (e _ {k}) = T ^ {*} (\alpha_ {k} e _ {k}) = | \alpha_ {k} | ^ {2} e _ {k} = T (\overline {{\alpha_ {k}}} e _ {k}) = (T T ^ {*}) (e _ {k}).
$$

Because the equation above holds for all $k \in \Gamma$ , we conclude that $T ^ { * } T = T T ^ { * } $ Thus T is normal, completing the proof of (b). 

The next result is one of the major highlights of the theory of compact operators on Hilbert spaces. The result as stated below applies to both real and complex Hilbert spaces. In the case of a real Hilbert space, the result below can be combined with 10.103(a) to produce the following result: A compact operator on a real Hilbert space is self-adjoint if and only if there is an orthonormal basis of the Hilbert space consisting of eigenvectors of the operator. 

10.106 Spectral Theorem for self-adjoint compact operators
Suppose T is a self-adjoint compact operator on a Hilbert space V. Then
(a) there is an orthonormal basis of V consisting of eigenvectors of T;
(b) there is a countable set $\Omega$ , an orthonormal family $\{e_{k}\}_{k\in\Omega}$ in V, and a family $\{\alpha_{k}\}_{k\in\Omega}$ in R $\setminus\{0\}$ such that $Tf = \sum_{k\in\Omega} \alpha_{k} \langle f, e_{k} \rangle e_{k}$ for every $f \in V$ . 

Proof Let U denote the span of all the eigenvectors of T. Then U is an invariant subspace for T. Hence $U ^ { \perp }$ is also an invariant subspace for T and $T | _ { U ^ { \perp } }$ is a selfadjoint operator on $U ^ { \perp }$ (by 10.102). However, $T | _ { U ^ { \rfloor } }$ has no eigenvalues, because all the eigenvectors of $T$ are in U. Because all self-adjoint compact operators on a nonzero Hilbert space have an eigenvalue (by 10.99), this implies that $U ^ { \perp } = \{ 0 \}$ Hence U = V (by 8.42). 

For each eigenvalue α of T, there is an orthonormal basis of null $\left( T - \alpha I \right)$ consisting of eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue α. The union (over all eigenvalues α of T) of all these orthonormal bases is an orthonormal family in V because eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal (see 10.57). The previous paragraph tells us that the closure of the span of this orthonormal family is V (here we are using the set itself as the index set). Hence we have an orthonormal basis of V consisting of eigenvectors of T, completing the proof of (a). 

By part (a) of this result, there is an orthonormal basis $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Gamma }$ of V and a family $\{ \alpha _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Gamma }$ in R such that $T e _ { k } = \alpha _ { k } e _ { k }$ for each $k \in \Gamma$ (even if ${ \bf F } = { \bf C }$ , the eigenvalues of $T$ are in R by 10.49) . Thus if $f \in V ,$ then 

$$
T f = T \Bigl (\sum_ {k \in \Gamma} \langle f, e _ {k} \rangle e _ {k} \Bigr) = \sum_ {k \in \Gamma} \langle f, e _ {k} \rangle T e _ {k} = \sum_ {k \in \Gamma} \alpha_ {k} \langle f, e _ {k} \rangle e _ {k}.
$$

Letting $\Omega = \{ k \in \Gamma : \alpha _ { k } \neq 0 \}$ , we can rewrite the equation above as 

$$
T f = \sum_ {k \in \Omega} \alpha_ {k} \langle f, e _ {k} \rangle e _ {k}
$$

for every $f \in V .$ The set Ω is countable because T has only countably many eigenvalues (by 10.93) and each nonzero eigenvalue can appear only finitely many times in the sum above (by 10.82), completing the proof of (b). 

A normal compact operator on a nonzero real Hilbert space might have no eigenvalues [consider, for example the normal operator T of counterclockwise rotation by a right angle on $\mathbf { R } ^ { 2 }$ defined by $T ( x , y ) = ( - y , x ) ]$ . However, the next result shows that normal compact operators on complex Hilbert spaces behave better. The key idea in proving this result is that on a complex Hilbert space, the real and imaginary parts of a normal compact operator are commuting self-adjoint compact operators, which then allows us to apply the Spectral Theorem for self-adjoint compact operators. 

## 10.107 Spectral Theorem for normal compact operators

Suppose T is a compact operator on a complex Hilbert space V. Then there is an orthonormal basis of V consisting of eigenvectors of T if and only if T is normal. 

Proof One direction of this result has already been proved as part (b) of 10.103. 

To prove the other direction, suppose T is a normal compact operator. We can write 

$$
T = A + i B,
$$

where A and B are self-adjoint operators and, because T is normal, $A B = B A$ (see 10.54). Because $A = ( T + T ^ { * } ) / 2$ and $B = ( T - T ^ { * } ) / ( 2 i )$ , the operators A and B are both compact. 

If $\alpha \in \mathbf { R }$ and $f \in \mathrm { n u l l } ( A - \alpha I )$ , then 

$$
(A - \alpha I) (B f) = A (B f) - \alpha B f = B (A f) - \alpha B f = B ((A - \alpha I) f) = B (0) = 0
$$

and thus $B f \in \mathrm { n u l l } ( A - \alpha I )$ . Hence null $\left( A - \alpha I \right)$ is an invariant subspace for B. Applying the Spectral Theorem for self-adjoint compact operators [10.106(a)] to $B | _ { \mathrm { n u l l } ( A - \alpha I ) }$ shows that for each eigenvalue α of $A$ , there is an orthonormal basis of $\mathrm { n u l l } ( A - \alpha I )$ consisting of eigenvectors of B. The union (over all eigenvalues α of A) of all these orthonormal bases is an orthonormal family in $V$ (use the set itself as the index set) because eigenvectors of A corresponding to distinct eigenvalues of A are orthogonal (see 10.57). The Spectral Theorem for self-adjoint compact operators [10.106(a)] as applied to A tells us that the closure of the span of this orthonormal family is V. Hence we have an orthonormal basis of $V ,$ each of whose elements is an eigenvector of A and an eigenvector of B. 

If $f \in V$ is an eigenvector of both A and B, then there exist $\alpha , \beta \in \mathbf { R }$ such that $A f = \alpha f$ and $B f = \beta f$ . Thus $T f = ( A + i B ) ( f ) = ( \alpha + \beta i ) { \dot { f } } ;$ ; hence $f$ is an eigenvector of T. Thus the orthonormal basis of V constructed in the previous paragraph is an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of $T _ { \ast }$ , completing the proof. 

The following example shows the power of the Spectral Theorem for normal compact operators. Finding the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the normal compact operator $\nu - \nu ^ { * }$ in the next example leads us to an orthonormal basis of $L ^ { 2 } ( [ 0 , 1 ] )$ Easy calculus shows that the family $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \mathbf { Z } }$ , where $e _ { k }$ is defined as in 10.112, is an orthonormal family in $L ^ { 2 } ( [ 0 , 1 ] )$ . The hard part of showing that $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \mathbf { Z } }$ is an orthonormal basis of $\mathring { L } ^ { 2 } ( [ 0 , 1 ] )$ is to show that the closure of the span of this family is $L ^ { 2 } ( [ 0 , 1 ] )$ ). However, the Spectral Theorem for normal compact operators (10.107) provides this information with no further work required. 

10.108 Example an orthonormal basis ofeigenvectors 

Suppose  : $L ^ { 2 } ( [ 0 , 1 ] ) \to L ^ { 2 } ( [ 0 , 1 ] )$ is the Volterra operator defined by 

$$
(\mathcal {V} f) (x) = \int_ {0} ^ {x} f.
$$

The operator is compact (see the paragraph after the proof of 10.70), but it is not normal. Because $\nu$ is compact, so is $\mathcal { V } ^ { \ast }$ (by 10.73). Hence $\nu - \nu ^ { * }$ is compact. Also, $( \mathcal { V } - \mathcal { V } ^ { * } ) ^ { * } = \mathcal { V } ^ { * } - \mathcal { V } = - ( \mathcal { V } - \mathcal { V } ^ { * } )$ . Because every operator commutes with its negative, we conclude that $\nu - \nu ^ { * }$ is a compact normal operator. Because we want to apply the Spectral Theorem, for the rest of this example we will take ${ \bf F } = { \bf C }$ 

If $f \in L ^ { 2 } ( [ 0 , 1 ] )$ and $x \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ , then the formula for $\mathcal { V } ^ { \ast }$ given by 10.16 shows that 

10.109 

$$
\big ((\mathcal {V} - \mathcal {V} ^ {*}) f \big) (x) = 2 \int_ {0} ^ {x} f - \int_ {0} ^ {1} f.
$$

The right side of the equation above is a continuous function of x whose value at $x = 0$ is the negative of its value at $x = 1$ 

Differentiating both sides of the equation above and using the Lebesgue Differentiation Theorem (4.19) shows that 

$$
\left((\mathcal {V} - \mathcal {V} ^ {*}) f\right) ^ {\prime} (x) = 2 f (x)
$$

for almost every $x \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ . If $f \in \mathrm { n u l l } ( \mathcal { V } - \mathcal { V } ^ { * } )$ , then differentiating both sides of the equation $( \mathcal { V } - \mathcal { V } ^ { * } ) \bar { f } = \bar { 0 }$ shows that $2 f ( x ) = 0$ for almost every $x \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ ; hence $f = 0 ;$ , and we conclude that $\nu - \nu ^ { * }$ is injective (so 0 is not an eigenvalue). 

Suppose $f$ is an eigenvector of $\nu - \nu ^ { * }$ with eigenvalue α. Thus $f$ is in the range of $\nu - \nu ^ { * } ,$ , which by 10.109 implies that $f$ is continuous on $[ 0 , 1 ]$ , which by 10.109 again implies that $f$ is continuously differentiable on $( 0 , 1 )$ . Differentiating both sides of the equation $( \mathcal { V } - \mathcal { V } ^ { * } ) f = \alpha f$ gives 

$$
2 f (x) = \alpha f ^ {\prime} (x)
$$

for all $x \in ( 0 , 1 )$ . Hence the function whose value at x is $e ^ { - ( 2 / \alpha ) x } f ( x )$ has derivative 0 everywhere on (0, 1) and thus is a constant function. In other words, 

$$
f (x) = c e ^ {(2 / \alpha) x}\tag{10.110}
$$

for some constant $c \neq 0$ . Because $f \in \mathrm { r a n g e } ( V - \mathcal { V } ^ { * } )$ , we have $f ( 0 ) = - f ( 1 )$ which with the equation above implies that there exists $k \in \mathbf { Z }$ such that 

$$
2 / \alpha = i (2 k + 1) \pi .\tag{10.111}
$$

Replacing $2 / \alpha$ in 10.110 with the value of $2 / \alpha$ derived in 10.111 shows that for $k \in \mathbf { Z } .$ , we should define $e _ { k } \in L ^ { 2 } ( [ 0 , 1 ] )$ by 

$$
e _ {k} (x) = e ^ {i (2 k + 1) \pi x}.\tag{10.112}
$$

Clearly $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \mathbf { Z } }$ is an orthonormal family in $L ^ { 2 } ( [ 0 , 1 ] )$ [the orthogonality can be verified by a straightforward calculation or by using 10.57]. The paragraph above and the Spectral Theorem for compact normal operators (10.107) imply that this orthonormal family is an orthonormal basis of $L ^ { 2 } ( [ 0 , 1 ] )$ 

## Singular Value Decomposition

The next result provides an important generalization of 10.106(b) to arbitrary compact operators that need not be self-adjoint or normal. This generalization requires two orthonormal families, as compared to the single orthonormal family in 10.106(b). 

## 10.113 Singular Value Decomposition

Suppose T is a compact operator on a Hilbert space V. Then there exist a countable set Ω, orthonormal families $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Omega }$ and $\{ h _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Omega }$ in $V ,$ and a family $\{ s _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Omega }$ of positive numbers such that 

10.114 

$$
T f = \sum_ {k \in \Omega} s _ {k} \langle f, e _ {k} \rangle h _ {k}
$$

for every $f \in V .$ 

Proof If α is an eigenvalue of $T ^ { * } T$ , then $( T ^ { * } T ) f = \alpha f$ for some $f \neq 0$ and 

$$
\alpha \| f \| ^ {2} = \langle \alpha f, f \rangle = \langle T ^ {*} T f, f \rangle = \langle T f, T f \rangle = \| T f \| ^ {2}.
$$

Thus $\alpha \geq 0$ . Hence all eigenvalues of $T ^ { * } T$ are nonnegative. 

Apply 10.106(b) and the conclusion of the paragraph above to the self-adjoint compact operator $T ^ { * } T$ , getting a countable set Ω, an orthonormal family $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Omega }$ in $V ,$ and a family $\{ s _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Omega }$ of positive numbers (take $s _ { k } = \sqrt { \alpha _ { k } } )$ such that 

10.115 

$$
(T ^ {*} T) f = \sum_ {k \in \Omega} s _ {k} ^ {2} \langle f, e _ {k} \rangle e _ {k}
$$

for every $f \in V .$ The equation above implies that $( T ^ { * } T ) e _ { j } = s _ { j } { } ^ { 2 } e _ { j }$ for each $j \in \Omega$ 

For $k \in \Omega$ , let 

$$
h _ {k} = \frac {T e _ {k}}{s _ {k}}.
$$

For $j , k \in \Omega$ , we have 

$$
\langle h _ {j}, h _ {k} \rangle = \frac {1}{s _ {j} s _ {k}} \langle T e _ {j}, T e _ {k} \rangle = \frac {1}{s _ {j} s _ {k}} \langle T ^ {*} T e _ {j}, e _ {k} \rangle = \frac {s _ {j}}{s _ {k}} \langle e _ {j}, e _ {k} \rangle .
$$

The equation above implies that $\{ h _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Omega }$ is an orthonormal family in V. 

If $f \in \mathrm { s p a n } \left\{ e _ { k } \right\} _ { k \in \Omega }$ , then 

$$
T f = T \left(\sum_ {k \in \Omega} \langle f, e _ {k} \rangle e _ {k}\right) = \sum_ {k \in \Omega} \langle f, e _ {k} \rangle T e _ {k} = \sum_ {k \in \Omega} s _ {k} \langle f, e _ {k} \rangle h _ {k},
$$

showing that 10.114 holds for such $f .$ 

If $f \in ( \overline { { \mathrm { s p a n } \left\{ e _ { k } \right\} _ { k \in \Omega } } } ) ^ { \perp }$ , then 10.115 shows that $( T ^ { * } T ) f = 0$ , which implies that $T f = 0$ (because $0 = \langle T ^ { * } T f , f \rangle = \| T f \| ^ { 2 } )$ ; thus both sides of 10.114 are 0. 

Hence the two sides of 10.114 agree for f in a closed subspace of V and for f in the orthogonal complement of that closed subspace, which by linearity implies that the two sides of 10.114 agree for all $f \in V .$ 

An expression of the form 10.114 is called a singular value decomposition of the compact operator T. The orthonormal families $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Omega }$ and $\{ h _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Omega }$ in the singular value decomposition are not uniquely determined by $T .$ . However, the positive numbers $\{ s _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Omega }$ are uniquely determined as positive square roots of positive eigenvalues of $T ^ { * } T$ . These positive numbers can be placed in decreasing order (because if there are infinitely many of them, then they form a sequence with limit 0, by 10.93). This procedure leads to the definition of singular values given below. 

Suppose $T$ is a compact operator. Recall that the geometric multiplicity of a positive eigenvalue $\alpha$ of $T ^ { * } T$ is defined to be dim null $\left( T ^ { * } T - \alpha I \right)$ [see 10.81]. This geometric multiplicity is the number of times that $\sqrt { \alpha }$ appears in the family $\{ s _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Omega }$ corresponding to a singular value decomposition of T. By 10.82, this geometric multiplicity is finite. 

Now we can define the singular values of a compact operator $T ,$ where we are careful to repeat the square root of each positive eigenvalue of $T ^ { * } T$ as many times as its geometric multiplicity. 

10.116 Definition singular values
- Suppose $T$ is a compact operator on a Hilbert space. The singular values of $T$ , denoted $s_1(T) \geq s_2(T) \geq s_3(T) \geq \cdots$ , are the positive square roots of the positive eigenvalues of $T^*T$ , arranged in decreasing order with each singular value $s$ repeated as many times as the geometric multiplicity of $s^2$ as an eigenvalue of $T^*T$ .
- If $T^*T$ has only finitely many positive eigenvalues, then define $s_n(T) = 0$ for all $n \in \mathbf{Z}^+$ for which $s_n(T)$ is not defined by the first bullet point. 

## 10.117 Example singular values on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space

Define T : $\mathbf { F } ^ { 4 } \to \mathbf { F } ^ { 4 }$ by 

$$
T (z _ {1}, z _ {2}, z _ {3}, z _ {4}) = (0, 3 z _ {1}, 2 z _ {2}, - 3 z _ {4}).
$$

A calculation shows that 

$$
(T ^ {*} T) (z _ {1}, z _ {2}, z _ {3}, z _ {4}) = (9 z _ {1}, 4 z _ {2}, 0, 9 z _ {4}).
$$

Thus the eigenvalues of $T ^ { * } T$ are $9 , 4 , 0$ and 

$$
\dim (T ^ {*} T - 9 I) = 2 \quad \text { and } \quad \dim (T ^ {*} T - 4 I) = 1.
$$

Taking square roots of the positive eigenvalues of $T ^ { * } T$ and then adjoining an infinite string of $0 \mathrm { { s } }$ shows that the singular values of $T$ are $3 \geq 3 \geq 2 \geq 0 \geq 0 \geq \cdot \cdot \cdot$ 

Note that $^ { - 3 }$ and 0 are the only eigenvalues of T. Thus in this case, the list of eigenvalues of T did not pick up the number 2 that appears in the definition (and hence the behavior) of $T ,$ but the list of singular values of T does include 2. 

If T is a compact operator, then the first singular value $s _ { 1 } ( T )$ equals $\| T \|$ , as you are asked to verify in Exercise 12. 

10.118 Example singular values of $\nu - \nu ^ { * }$ 

Let denote the Volterra operator and let $T = \mathcal { V } - \mathcal { V } ^ { * } .$ . In Example 10.108, we saw that if $e _ { k }$ is defined by 10.112 then $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \mathbf { Z } }$ is an orthonormal basis of $L ^ { 2 } ( [ 0 , 1 ] )$ 1 and 

$$
T e _ {k} = \frac {2}{i (2 k + 1) \pi} e _ {k}
$$

for each $k \in \mathbf { Z } .$ , where the eigenvalue shown above corresponding to $e _ { k }$ comes from 10.111. Now 10.56 implies that 

$$
T ^ {*} e _ {k} = \frac {- 2}{i (2 k + 1) \pi} e _ {k}
$$

for each $k \in \mathbf { Z }$ . Hence 

10.119 

$$
T ^ {*} T e _ {k} = \frac {4}{(2 k + 1) ^ {2} \pi^ {2}} e _ {k}
$$

for each $k \in \mathbf { Z }$ . After taking positive square roots of the eigenvalues, we see that the equation above shows that the singular values of T are 

$$
{\frac {2}{\pi}} \geq {\frac {2}{\pi}} \geq {\frac {2}{3 \pi}} \geq {\frac {2}{3 \pi}} \geq {\frac {2}{5 \pi}} \geq {\frac {2}{5 \pi}} \geq \dots ,
$$

where the first two singular values above come from taking $k = - 1$ and $k = 0$ in 10.119, the next two singular values above come from taking $k = - 2$ and $k = 1$ the next two singular values above come from taking $k = - 3$ and $k = 2$ , and so on. Each singular value of T appears twice in the list of singular values above because each eigenvalue of $T ^ { * } T$ has geometric multiplicity 2. 

For $n \in \mathbf { Z } ^ { + } ,$ , the singular value $s _ { n } ( T )$ of a compact operator T tells us how well we can approximate $T$ by operators whose range has dimension less than n (see Exercise 15). 

The next result makes an important connection between $K \in L ^ { 2 } ( \mu \times \mu )$ and the singular values of the integral operator associated with K. 

10.120 sum of squares of singular values of integral operator
Suppose $\mu$ is a $\sigma$ -finite measure and $K \in L^{2}(\mu \times \mu)$ . Then $\|K\|_{L^{2}(\mu \times \mu)}^{2} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (s_{n}(\mathcal{I}_{K}))^{2}.$ 

Proof Consider a singular value decomposition 

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {K} (f) = \sum_ {k \in \Omega} s _ {k} \langle f, e _ {k} \rangle h _ {k}\tag{10.121}
$$

of the compact operator $\mathcal { T } _ { K }$ . Extend $\{ e _ { j } \} _ { j \in \Omega }$ to an orthonormal basis $\{ e _ { j } \} _ { j \in \Gamma }$ of $L ^ { 2 } ( \mu )$ , and extend $\{ h _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Omega }$ to an orthonormal basis $\{ h _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Gamma ^ { \prime } }$ of $L ^ { 2 } ( \mu )$ 

Let X denote the set on which the measure $\mu$ lives. For $j \in \Gamma$ and $k \in \Gamma ^ { \prime }$ , define $g _ { j , k } \colon X \times X \to \mathbf { F }$ by 

$$
g _ {j, k} (x, y) = \overline {{e _ {j} (y)}} h _ {k} (x).
$$

Then $\{ g _ { j , k } \} _ { j \in \Gamma , k \in \Gamma ^ { \prime } }$ is an orthonormal basis of $L ^ { 2 } ( \mu \times \mu )$ , as you should verify. Thus 

10.122 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \| K \| _ {L ^ {2} (\mu \times \mu)} ^ {2} = \sum_ {j \in \Gamma , k \in \Gamma^ {\prime}} | \langle K, g _ {j, k} \rangle | ^ {2} \\ \qquad = \sum_ {j \in \Gamma , k \in \Gamma^ {\prime}} \left| \int \int K (x, y) e _ {j} (y) \overline {{h _ {k} (x)}}   d \mu (y)   d \mu (x) \right| ^ {2} \\ \qquad = \sum_ {j \in \Gamma , k \in \Gamma^ {\prime}} \left| \int (\mathcal {I} _ {K} e _ {j}) (x) \overline {{h _ {k} (x)}}   d \mu (x) \right| ^ {2} \\ \qquad = \sum_ {j \in \Omega , k \in \Gamma^ {\prime}} \left| \int s _ {j} h _ {j} (x) \overline {{h _ {k} (x)}}   d \mu (x) \right| ^ {2} \\ \qquad = \sum_ {j \in \Omega} s _ {j} ^ {2} \\ \qquad = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \left(s _ {n} (\mathcal {I} _ {K})\right) ^ {2}, \end{array}
$$

10.123 

where 10.122 holds because 10.121 shows that $\mathcal { T } _ { K } e _ { j } = s _ { j } h _ { j }$ for $j \in \Omega$ and $\mathcal { T } _ { K } e _ { j } = 0$ for $j \in \Gamma \setminus \Omega$ ; 10.123 holds because $\{ h _ { k } \} _ { k \in \Gamma ^ { \prime } }$ is an orthonormal family. 

Now we can give a spectacular application of the previous result. 

10.124 Example ${ \frac { 1 } { 1 ^ { 2 } } } + { \frac { 1 } { 3 ^ { 2 } } } + { \frac { 1 } { 5 ^ { 2 } } } + \cdot \cdot \cdot = { \frac { \pi ^ { 2 } } { 8 } }$ 

Define $K \colon [ 0 , 1 ] \times [ 0 , 1 ] \to \mathbf { R }$ by 

$$
K (x, y) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & \text { if } x > y, \\ 0 & \text { if } x = y, \\ - 1 & \text { if } x <   y. \end{array} \right.
$$

Letting $\mu$ be Lebesgue measure on $[ 0 , 1 ]$ , we note that $\mathcal { T } _ { K }$ is the normal compact operator $\nu - \nu ^ { * }$ examined in Example 10.118. 

Clearly $\| K \| _ { L ^ { 2 } ( \mu \times \mu ) } = 1$ . Using the list of singular values for $\mathcal { T } _ { K }$ obtained in Example 10.118, the formula in 10.120 tells us that 

$$
1 = 2 \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {4}{(2 k + 1) ^ {2} \pi^ {2}}.
$$

Thus 

$$
\frac {1}{1 ^ {2}} + \frac {1}{3 ^ {2}} + \frac {1}{5 ^ {2}} + \dots = \frac {\pi^ {2}}{8}.
$$

## EXERCISES 10D

1 Prove that if T is a compact operator on a nonzero Hilbert space, then $\| T \| ^ { 2 }$ is an eigenvalue of $T ^ { * } T$ 

2 Prove that if T is a self-adjoint operator on a nonzero Hilbert space V, then 

$$
\| T \| = \sup \left\{\left| \langle T f, f \rangle \right|: f \in V \text {   and   } \| f \| = 1 \right\}.
$$

3 Suppose T is a bounded operator on a Hilbert space V and U is a closed subspace of V. Prove that the following are equivalent: 

(a) U is an invariant subspace for T. 

(b) $U ^ { \perp }$ is an invariant subspace for $T ^ { * }$ . 

(c) $T P _ { U } = P _ { U } T P _ { U } .$ 

4 Suppose T is a bounded operator on a Hilbert space V and U is a closed subspace of V. Prove that the following are equivalent: 

(a) U and $U ^ { \perp }$ are invariant subspaces for T. 

(b) U and $U ^ { \perp }$ are invariant subspaces for $T ^ { * }$ 

(c) $T P _ { U } = P _ { U } T .$ 

5 Suppose T is a bounded operator on a nonseparable normed vector space V. Prove that T has a closed invariant subspace other than 0 and V. 

6 Suppose T is an operator on a Banach space V with dimension greater than 2. Prove that T has an invariant subspace other than 0 and V. [For this exercise, T is not assumed to be bounded and the invariant subspace is not required to be closed.] 

7 Suppose T is a self-adjoint compact operator on a Hilbert space that has only finitely many distinct eigenvalues. Prove that T has finite-dimensional range. 

8 (a) Prove that if T is a self-adjoint compact operator on a Hilbert space, then there exists a self-adjoint compact operator S such that $S ^ { 3 } = T$ 

(b) Prove that if T is a normal compact operator on a complex Hilbert space, then there exists a normal compact operator S such that $S ^ { 2 } = T$ 

9 Suppose T is a compact normal operator on a nonzero Hilbert space V. Prove that there is a subspace of V with dimension 1 or 2 that is an invariant subspace for T. 

[If F = C, the desired result follows immediately from the Spectral Theorem for compact normal operators. Thus you can assume that $\mathbf { F } = \mathbf { R } . ]$ 

10 Suppose T is a self-adjoint compact operator on a Hilbert space and $\textstyle \left\| T \right\| \leq { \frac { 1 } { 4 } }$ Prove that there exists a self-adjoint compact operator S such that $S ^ { 2 } + S = { \bar { T } }$ 

11 For $k \in \mathbf { Z }$ , define $g _ { k } \in L ^ { 2 } { \big ( } { \big ( } - \pi , \pi ] { \big ) } \ \mathrm { a n d } \ h _ { k } \in L ^ { 2 } { \big ( } { \big ( } - \pi , \pi ] { \big ) }$ by 

$$

# Chapter 11 Fourier Analysis

This chapter uses Hilbert space theory to motivate the introduction of Fourier coeffi cients and Fourier series. The classical setting applies these concepts to functions defined on bounded intervals of the real line. However, the theory becomes easier and cleaner when we instead use a modern approach by considering functions defined on the unit circle of the complex plane. 

The first section of this chapter shows how consideration of Fourier series leads us to harmonic functions and a solution to the Dirichlet problem. In the second section of this chapter, convolution becomes a major tool for the $L ^ { p }$ theory. 

The third section of this chapter changes the context to functions defined on the real line. Many of the techniques introduced in the first two sections of the chapter transfer easily to provide results about the Fourier transform on the real line. The highlights of our treatment of the Fourier transform are the Fourier Inversion Formula and the extension of the Fourier transform to a unitary operator on $L ^ { 2 } ( \mathbf { R } )$ 

The vast field of Fourier analysis cannot be completely covered in a single chapter. Thus this chapter gives readers just a taste of the subject. Readers who go on from this chapter to one of the many book-length treatments of Fourier analysis will then already be familiar with the terminology and techniques of the subject. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/dd468151-b8ed-4849-9b9d-66f1c76294ba/47714007f8d3acd4c7a15afdd29acbbc7f2cc1839eb1d2332ab9af69b6e3a4ca.jpg)


The Giza pyramids, near where the Battle ofPyramids took place in 1798 during Napoleon’s invasion ofEgypt. Joseph Fourier (1768–1830) was one ofthe scientific advisors to Napoleon in Egypt. While in Egypt as part ofNapoleon’s invadingforce, Fourier began thinking about the mathematical theory ofheat propagation, which eventually led to what we now call Fourier series and the Fourier transform. 

# 11A Fourier Series and Poisson Integral

## Fourier Coefficients and Riemann–Lebesgue Lemma

For $k \in \mathbf { Z }$ , suppose $e _ { k } \colon ( - \pi , \pi ] \to \mathbf { R }$ is defined by 

$$
e _ {k} (t) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \frac {1}{\sqrt {\pi}} \sin (k t) & \text {if k > 0 ,} \\ \frac {1}{\sqrt {2 \pi}} & \text {if k = 0 ,} \\ \frac {1}{\sqrt {\pi}} \cos (k t) & \text {if k <   0 .} \end{array} \right.\tag{11.1}
$$

The classical theory of Fourier series features $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \mathbf { Z } }$ as an orthonormal basis of $L ^ { 2 } { \bigl ( } ( - \pi , \pi ] { \bigr ) }$ . The trigonometric formulas displayed in Exercise 1 in Section 8C can be used to show that $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \mathbf { Z } }$ is indeed an orthonormal family in $L ^ { 2 } { \bigl ( } ( - \pi , \pi ] { \bigr ) }$ 

To show that $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \mathbf { Z } }$ is an orthonormal basis of $L ^ { 2 } { \bigl ( } ( - \pi , \pi ] { \bigr ) }$ requires more work. One slick possibility is to note that the Spectral Theorem for compact operators produces orthonormal bases; an appropriate choice of a compact normal operator can then be used to show that $\{ e _ { k } \} _ { k \in \mathbf { Z } }$ is an orthonormal basis of $L ^ { 2 } { \big ( } ( - \pi , { \bar { \pi } } ] { \big ) }$ [see Exercise 11(c) in Section 10D]. 

In this chapter we take a cleaner approach to Fourier series by working on the unit circle in the complex plane instead of on the interval $\left( - \pi , \pi \right]$ . The map 

## 11.2

$$
t \mapsto e ^ {i t} = \cos t + i \sin t
$$

can be used to identify the interval $\left( - \pi , \pi \right]$ with the unit circle; thus the two approaches are equivalent. However, the calculations are easier in the unit circle context. In addition, we will see that the unit circle context provides the huge benefit of making a connection with harmonic functions. 

We begin by introducing notation for the open unit disk and the unit circle in the complex plane. 

## 11.3 Definition D; ∂D

D denotes the open unit disk in the complex plane: 

$$
\mathbf {D} = \{w \in \mathbf {C}: | w | <   1 \}.
$$

∂D is the unit circle in the complex plane: 

$$
\partial \mathbf {D} = \{z \in \mathbf {C}: | z | = 1 \}.
$$

The function given in 11.2 is a one-to-one map of $\left( - \pi , \pi \right]$ onto ∂D. We use this map to define a σ-algebra on ∂D by transferring the Borel subsets of $( - \pi , \pi ]$ to subsets of ∂D that we will call the measurable subsets of ∂D. We also transfer Lebesgue measure on the Borel subsets of $( \pi , \pi ]$ to a measure called $\sigma$ on the measurable subsets of ∂D, except that for convenience we normalize by dividing by $2 \pi$ so that the measure of ∂D is 1 rather than $2 \pi$ . We are now ready to give the formal definitions. 

11.4 Definition measurable subsets of $\partial D$ ; $\sigma$ • A subset E of $\partial D$ is measurable if $\{t \in (-\pi, \pi] : e^{it} \in E\}$ is a Borel subset of R.

• $\sigma$ is the measure on the measurable subsets of $\partial D$ obtained by transferring Lebesgue measure from $(-\pi, \pi]$ to $\partial D$ , normalized so that $\sigma(\partial D) = 1$ . In other words, if $E \subset \partial D$ is measurable, then $\sigma(E) = \frac{|\{t \in (-\pi, \pi] : e^{it} \in E\}|}{2\pi}$ .

Our definition of the measure $\sigma$ on $\partial D$ allows us to transfer integration on $\partial D$ to the familiar context of integration on $(-\pi, \pi]$ . Specifically, $\int_{\partial D} f d\sigma = \int_{\partial D} f(z) d\sigma(z) = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(e^{it}) \frac{dt}{2\pi}$ for all measurable functions $f: \partial D \to C$ such that any of these integrals is defined. Throughout this chapter, we assume that the scalar field F is the complex field C. Furthermore, $L^{p}(\partial D)$ is defined as follows.

11.5 Definition $L^{p}(\partial D)$ For $1 \leq p \leq \infty$ , define $L^{p}(\partial D)$ to mean the complex version (F = C) of $L^{p}(\sigma)$ .

Note that if $z = e^{it}$ for some $t \in R$ , then $\bar{z} = e^{-it} = \frac{1}{z}$ and $z^{n} = e^{int}$ and $\overline{z^{n}} = e^{-int}$ for all $n \in Z$ . These observations make the proof of the next result much simpler than the proof of the corresponding result for the trigonometric family defined by 11.1.

In the statement of the next result, $z^{n}$ means the function on $\partial D$ defined by $z \mapsto z^{n}$ .

11.6 orthonormal family in $L^{2}(\partial D)$ $\{z^{n}\}_{n \in Z}$ is an orthonormal family in $L^{2}(\partial D)$ .

Proof If $n \in Z$ , then $\langle z^{n}, z^{n} \rangle = \int_{\partial D} |z^{n}|^{2} d\sigma(z) = \int_{\partial D} 1 d\sigma = 1.$ If $m, n \in Z$ with $m \neq n$ , then $\langle z^{m}, z^{n} \rangle = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} e^{imt} e^{-int} \frac{dt}{2\pi} = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} e^{i(m-n)t} \frac{dt}{2\pi} = \frac{e^{i(m-n)t}}{i(m-n)2\pi} \bigg]_{t=-\pi}^{t=\pi} = 0,$ as desired.

In the next section, we improve the result above by showing that $\{z^{n}\}_{n \in Z}$ is an orthonormal basis of $L^{2}(\partial D)$ (see 11.30). 

Hilbert space theory tells us that if f is in the closure in $L ^ { 2 } ( \partial { \bf D } )$ of span $\{ z ^ { n } \} _ { n \in \mathbf { Z } }$ then 

$$
f = \sum_ {n \in \mathbf {Z}} \langle f, z ^ {n} \rangle z ^ {n},
$$

where the infinite sum above converges as an unordered sum in the norm of $L ^ { 2 } ( \partial { \bf D } )$ (see 8.58). The inner product $\left. f , z ^ { n } \right.$ above equals 

$$
\int_ {\partial \mathbf {D}} f (z) \overline {{z ^ {n}}} d \sigma (z).
$$

Because $\left| z ^ { n } \right| = 1$ for every $z \in \partial \mathbf { D }$ , the integral above makes sense not only for $f \in L ^ { 2 } ( \partial \mathbf { \dot { D } } )$ but also for f in the larger space $\bar { L } ^ { 1 } ( \partial \mathbf { D } )$ . Thus we make the following definition. 

11.7 Definition Fourier coefficient
Suppose $f \in L^{1}(\partial\mathbf{D})$ .
• For $n \in Z$ , the $n^{th}$ Fourier coefficient of f is denoted $\hat{f}(n)$ and is defined by $\hat{f}(n)=\int_{\partial\mathbf{D}}f(z)\overline{z^{n}}d\sigma(z)=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}f(e^{it})e^{-int}\frac{dt}{2\pi}.$ • The Fourier series of f is the formal sum $\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}\hat{f}(n)z^{n}.$ 

As we will see, Fourier analysis helps describe the sense in which the Fourier series of f represents $f .$ 

## 11.8 Example Fourier coefficients

Suppose $h$ is an analytic function on an open set that contains ${ \overline { { D } } } .$ . Then h has a power series representation 

$$
h (z) = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} a _ {n} z ^ {n},
$$

where the sum on the right converges uniformly on $\overline { { D } }$ to $h .$ . Because uniform convergence on ∂D implies convergence in $L ^ { 2 } ( \partial \mathbf { \bar { D } } )$ , 8.58(b) and 11.6 now imply that 

$$
(h | _ {\partial \mathbf {D}}) ^ {\wedge} (n) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} a _ {n} & \text { if } n \geq 0, \\ 0 & \text { if } n <   0 \end{array} \right.
$$

for all $n \in \mathbf { Z }$ . In other words, for functions analytic on an open set containing ${ \overline { { D } } } .$ , the Fourier series is the same as the Taylor series. 

• <sup>Suppose</sup> $f \colon \partial \mathbf { D }  \mathbf { R } \quad$ is defined by 

$$
f (z) = \frac {1}{| 3 - z | ^ {2}}.
$$

Then for $z \in \partial \mathbf { D }$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & f (z) = \frac {1}{(3 - z) (3 - \overline {{z}})} \\ & \qquad = \frac {1}{8} \Big (\frac {z}{3 - z} + \frac {3}{3 - \overline {{z}}} \Big) \\ & \qquad = \frac {1}{8} \Big (\frac {\frac {z}{3}}{1 - \frac {z}{3}} + \frac {1}{1 - \frac {\overline {{z}}}{3}} \Big) \\ & \qquad = \frac {1}{8} \Big (\frac {z}{3} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {z ^ {n}}{3 ^ {n}} + \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {(\overline {{z}}) ^ {n}}{3 ^ {n}} \Big) \\ & \qquad = \frac {1}{8} \sum_ {n = - \infty} ^ {\infty} \frac {z ^ {n}}{3 ^ {| n |}}, \end{array}
$$

where the infinite sums above converge uniformly on ∂D. Thus we see that 

$$
\hat {f} (n) = \frac {1}{8} \cdot \frac {1}{3 ^ {| n |}}
$$

for all $n \in \mathbf { Z } .$ 

We begin with some simple algebraic properties of Fourier coefficients, whose proof is left to the reader. 

11.9 algebraic properties of Fourier coefficients
Suppose $f, g \in L^{1}(\partial\mathbf{D})$ and $n \in Z$ . Then
(a) $(f + g)^{(n)} = \hat{f}(n) + \hat{g}(n);$ (b) $(\alpha f)^{(n)} = \alpha \hat{f}(n)$ for all $\alpha \in C;$ (c) $|\hat{f}(n)| \leq \|f\|_{1}.$ 

Parts (a) and (b) above could be restated by saying that for each $n \in \mathbf { Z }$ , the function $f \mapsto { \hat { f } } ( n )$ is a linear functional from $L ^ { 1 } ( \partial \bar { \bf D } )$ to C. Part (c) could be restated by saying that this linear functional has norm at most 1. 

Part (c) above implies that the set of Fourier coefficients $\{ { \hat { f } } ( n ) \} _ { n \in \mathbf { Z } }$ is bounded for each $f \in L ^ { 1 } ( \partial \mathbf { D } )$ . The Fourier coefficients of the functions in Example 11.8 have the stronger property that $\textstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \pm \infty } { \hat { f } } ( n ) = 0$ . The next result shows that this stronger conclusion holds for all functions in $\dot { L } ^ { 1 } ( \partial \mathbf { D } )$ 

<table><tr><td>11.10 Riemann–Lebesgue Lemma</td></tr><tr><td>Suppose <eq>f \in L^{1}(\partial\mathbf{D})</eq>. Then <eq>\lim_{n \to \pm\infty} \hat{f}(n) = 0</eq>.</td></tr></table>

Proof Suppose $\varepsilon > 0 .$ . There exists $g \in L ^ { 2 } ( \partial \mathbf { D } )$ such that $\| f - g \| _ { 1 } < \varepsilon ( \boldsymbol { \mathrm { b y } } 3 . 4 4 )$ By 11.6 and Bessel’s inequality (8.57), we have 

$$
\sum_ {n = - \infty} ^ {\infty} | \hat {g} (n) | ^ {2} \leq \| g \| _ {2} ^ {2} <   \infty .
$$

Thus there exists $M \in { \mathbf { Z } } ^ { + }$ such that $| \hat { g } ( n ) | < \varepsilon$ for all $n \in \mathbf { Z }$ with $| n | \geq M$ . Now if $n \in \mathbf { Z }$ and $| n | \geq M$ , then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} | \hat {f} (n) | \leq | \hat {f} (n) - \hat {g} (n) | + | \hat {g} (n) | \\ <   | (f - g) ^ {\wedge} (n) | + \varepsilon \\ \leq \| f - g \| _ {1} + \varepsilon \\ <   2 \varepsilon . \end{array}
$$

Thus $\operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \pm \infty } { \hat { f } } ( n ) = 0 .$ 

## Poisson Kernel

Suppose $f \colon \partial \mathbf { D }  \mathbf { C }$ is continuous and $z \in \partial \mathbf { D }$ . For this fixed $z \in \partial \mathbf { D }$ , the Fourier series 

$$
\sum_ {n = - \infty} ^ {\infty} \hat {f} (n) z ^ {n}
$$

is a series of complex numbers. It would be nice if $\textstyle f ( z ) = \sum _ { n = - \infty } ^ { \infty } { \hat { f } } ( n ) z ^ { n }$ , but this is not necessarily true because the series $\scriptstyle \sum _ { n = - \infty } ^ { \infty } { \hat { f } } ( n ) z ^ { n }$ might not converge, as you can see in Exercise 11. 

Various techniques exist for trying to assign some meaning to a series of complex numbers that does not converge. In one such technique, called $A b e l$ summation, the $n ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ -term of the series is multiplied by $r ^ { n }$ and then the limit is taken as $r \uparrow 1$ . For example, if the $n ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ -term of the divergent series 

$$
1 - 1 + 1 - 1 + \dots
$$

is multiplied by $r ^ { n }$ for $r \in [ 0 , 1 )$ , we get a convergent series whose sum equals $\frac { r } { 1 + r }$ Taking the limit of this sum as $r \uparrow 1$ then gives $\frac 1 2$ as the value of the Abel sum of the series above. 

The next definition can be motivated by applying a similar technique to the Fourier series $\scriptstyle \sum _ { n = - \infty } ^ { \infty } { \hat { f } } ( n ) z ^ { n }$ . Here we have a series of complex numbers whose terms are indexed by $\mathbf { Z }$ rather than by ${ \mathbf Z } ^ { + }$ . Thus we use $r ^ { | n | }$ rather than $r ^ { n }$ because we want these multipliers to have limit 0 as $n  \pm \infty$ for each $r \in [ 0 , 1 )$ (and to have limit 1 as $r \uparrow 1$ for each $n \in \mathbf { Z } )$ 

<table><tr><td>11.11 Definition <eq>\mathcal{P}_{r}f</eq></td></tr><tr><td>For <eq>f \in L^{1}(\partial\mathbf{D})</eq> and <eq>0 \leq r &lt; 1</eq>, define <eq>\mathcal{P}_{r}f \colon \partial\mathbf{D} \to \mathbf{C}</eq> by<eq>(\mathcal{P}_{r}f)(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} r^{|n|}\hat{f}(n)z^{n}.</eq></td></tr></table>

No convergence problems arise in the series above because 

$$
\left| r ^ {| n |} \hat {f} (n) z ^ {n} \right| \leq \| f \| _ {1} r ^ {| n |}
$$

for each $z \in \partial \mathbf { D }$ , which implies that 

$$
\sum_ {n = - \infty} ^ {\infty} | r ^ {| n |} \hat {f} (n) z ^ {n} | \leq \| f \| _ {1} \frac {1 + r}{1 - r} <   \infty .
$$

Thus for each $r \in [ 0 , 1 )$ , the partial sums of the series above converge uniformly on ∂D, which implies that $\mathcal { P } _ { r } f$ is a continuous function from ∂D to $\mathbf { C }$ (for $r = 0$ and $n = 0$ , interpret the expression $0 ^ { 0 }$ to be 1). 

Let’s unravel the formula in 11.11. If $f \in L ^ { 1 } ( \partial \mathbf { D } ) , 0 \leq r < 1$ , and $z \in \partial \mathbf { D }$ , then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} (\mathcal {P} _ {r} f) (z) = \sum_ {n = - \infty} ^ {\infty} r ^ {| n |} \hat {f} (n) z ^ {n} \\ \qquad = \sum_ {n = - \infty} ^ {\infty} r ^ {| n |} \int_ {\partial \mathbf {D}} f (w) \overline {{w ^ {n}}} d \sigma (w) z ^ {n} \\ \qquad = \int_ {\partial \mathbf {D}} f (w) \Big (\sum_ {n = - \infty} ^ {\infty} r ^ {| n |} (z \overline {{w}}) ^ {n} \Big) d \sigma (w), \end{array}\tag{11.12}
$$

where interchanging the sum and integral above is justified by the uniform convergence of the series on ∂D. To evaluate the sum in parentheses in the last line above, let $\boldsymbol { \zeta } \in \partial \mathbf { D }$ (think of $\zeta = z { \overline { { w } } }$ in the formula above). Thus $( \zeta ) ^ { - n } = ( \overline { { \zeta } } ) ^ { n }$ and 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {n = - \infty} ^ {\infty} r ^ {| n |} \zeta^ {n} = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} (r \zeta) ^ {n} + \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} (r \overline {{\zeta}}) ^ {n} \\ \qquad = \frac {1}{1 - r \zeta} + \frac {r \overline {{\zeta}}}{1 - r \overline {{\zeta}}} \\ \qquad = \frac {(1 - r \overline {{\zeta}}) + (1 - r \zeta) r \overline {{\zeta}}}{| 1 - r \zeta | ^ {2}} \\ \qquad = \frac {1 - r ^ {2}}{| 1 - r \zeta | ^ {2}}. \end{array}\tag{11.13}
$$

Motivated by the formula above, we now make the following definition. Notice that 11.11 uses calligraphic $\mathcal { P } _ { \cdot }$ , while the next definition uses italic $P .$ 

11.14 Definition $P_{r}(\zeta)$ ; Poisson kernel

• For $0 \leq r < 1$ , define $P_{r} \colon \partial D \to (0, \infty)$ by $P_{r}(\zeta) = \frac{1 - r^{2}}{|1 - r\zeta|^{2}}.$ • The family of functions $\{P_{r}\}_{r \in [0,1)}$ is called the Poisson kernel on D. 

Combining 11.12 and 11.13 now gives the following result. 

11.15 integral formula for $P_{r}f$ If $f \in L^{1}(\partial\mathbf{D})$ , $0 \leq r < 1$ , and $z \in \partial D$ , then $(\mathcal{P}_{r}f)(z)=\int_{\partial\mathbf{D}}f(w)P_{r}(z\overline{w})d\sigma(w)=\int_{\partial\mathbf{D}}f(w)\frac{1-r^{2}}{|1-rz\overline{w}|^{2}}d\sigma(w).$ 

The terminology approximate identity is sometimes used to describe the three properties for the Poisson kernel given in the next result. 

11.16 properties of $P_{r}$ (a) $P_{r}(\zeta) > 0$ for all $r \in [0,1)$ and all $\zeta \in \partial D$ .

(b) $\int_{\partial D} P_{r}(\zeta) d\sigma(\zeta) = 1$ for each $r \in [0,1)$ .

(c) $\lim_{r \uparrow 1} \int_{\{\zeta \in \partial D : |1 - \zeta| \geq \delta\}} P_{r}(\zeta) d\sigma(\zeta) = 0$ for each $\delta > 0$ . 

Proof Part (a) follows immediately from the definition of $P _ { r } ( \zeta )$ given in 11.14. 

Part (b) follows from integrating the series representation for $P _ { r }$ given by 11.13 termwise and noting that 

$$
\int_ {\partial \mathbf {D}} \zeta^ {n} d \sigma (\zeta) = \int_ {- \pi} ^ {\pi} e ^ {i n t} \left. \frac {d t}{2 \pi} = \frac {e ^ {i n t}}{i n 2 \pi} \right] _ {t = - \pi} ^ {t = \pi} = 0 \text {for all} n \in \mathbf {Z} \setminus \{0 \};
$$

for $n = 0 .$ , we have $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { \partial \mathbf { D } } \zeta ^ { n } d \sigma ( \zeta ) = 1 . } \end{array}$ 

To prove part (c), suppose $\delta > 0 .$ . If $\zeta \in \partial \mathbf { D } , | 1 - \zeta | \geq \delta$ , and $\begin{array} { r } { 1 - r < \frac { \delta } { 2 } } \end{array}$ , then 

$$
\begin{array}{c} | 1 - r \zeta | = | 1 - \zeta - (r - 1) \zeta | \\ \geq | 1 - \zeta | - (1 - r) \\ > \frac {\delta}{2}. \end{array}
$$

Thus as $r \uparrow 1$ , the denominator in the definition of $P _ { r } ( \zeta )$ is uniformly bounded away from 0 on $\left\{ \zeta \in \partial \mathbf { D } : | 1 - \zeta | \geq \delta \right\}$ and the numerator goes to 0. Thus the integral of $P _ { r }$ over $\left\{ \zeta \in \partial \mathbf { D } : | 1 - \zeta | \geq \delta \right\}$ goes to 0 as $r \uparrow 1$ 

Here is the intuition behind the proof of the next result: Parts (a) and (b) of the previous result and 11.15 mean that $( \mathcal { P } _ { r } f ) ( z )$ is a weighted average of $f$ . Part (c) of the previous result says that for r close to 1, most of the weight in this weighted average is concentrated near z. Thus $( { \mathcal { P } } _ { r } f ) ( z ) \to f ( z )$ as $r \uparrow 1$ 

The figure here transfers the context from ∂D to $( - \pi , \pi ]$ . The area under both curves is $2 \pi$ [corresponding to 11.16(b)] and $P _ { r } ( e ^ { i t } )$ becomes more concentrated near $t = 0$ as r 1 [corresponding to 11.16(c)]. See Exercise 3 for the formula for $P _ { r } ( e ^ { i t } )$

11.18 if f is continuous, then $\lim_{r\uparrow1}\|f-\mathcal{P}_{r}f\|_{\infty}=0$ Suppose $f: \partial D \to C$ is continuous. Then $P_{r}f$ converges uniformly to f on $\partial D$ as $r \uparrow 1$ . 

Proof Suppose $\varepsilon > 0$ . Because f is uniformly continuous on ∂D, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that 

$$
\left| f (z) - f (w) \right| <   \varepsilon \text {   for   all   } z, w \in \partial \mathbf {D} \text {   with   } | z - w | <   \delta .
$$

$\mathbf { I f } ~ z \in \partial \mathbf { D }$ , then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} | f (z) - (\mathcal {P} _ {r} f) (z) | = \left| f (z) - \int_ {\partial \mathbf {D}} f (w) P _ {r} (z \overline {{w}}) d \sigma (w) \right| \\ \qquad = \left| \int_ {\partial \mathbf {D}} \bigl (f (z) - f (w) \bigr) P _ {r} (z \overline {{w}}) d \sigma (w) \right| \\ \qquad \leq \varepsilon \int_ {\{w \in \partial \mathbf {D}: | z - w | <   \delta \}} P _ {r} (z \overline {{w}}) d \sigma (w) \\ \qquad + 2 \| f \| _ {\infty} \int_ {\{w \in \partial \mathbf {D}: | z - w | \geq \delta \}} P _ {r} (z \overline {{w}}) d \sigma (w) \\ \qquad \leq \varepsilon + 2 \| f \| _ {\infty} \int_ {\{\zeta \in \partial \mathbf {D}: | 1 - \zeta | \geq \delta \}} P _ {r} (\zeta) d \sigma (\zeta), \end{array}
$$

where we have used 11.17, 11.16(a), and 11.16(b); the last line uses the equality $| z - w | = | 1 - \zeta |$ , which holds when $\zeta = z { \overline { { w } } }$ . Now 11.16(c) shows that the value of the last integral above has uniform (with respect to $z \in \partial \mathbf { D } )$ limit 0 as $r \uparrow 1$ 

## Solution to Dirichlet Problem on Disk

As a bonus to our investigation into Fourier series, the previous result provides the solution to the Dirichlet problem on the unit disk. To state the Dirichlet problem, we first need a few definitions. As usual, we identify C with $\mathbf { R } ^ { 2 }$ . Thus for $\cdot , y \in \mathbf { R }$ , we can think of $w = x + y i \in \mathbf { C }$ or $w = ( x , y ) \in \mathbf { R } ^ { 2 }$ . Hence 

$$
\mathbf {D} = \{w \in \mathbf {C}: | w | <   1 \} = \{(x, y) \in \mathbf {R} ^ {2}: x ^ {2} + y ^ {2} <   1 \}.
$$

For a function $f \colon G \to \mathbf { C }$ on an open subset $G$ of C (or an open subset $G$ of $\mathbf { R } ^ { 2 } )$ , the partial derivatives $D _ { 1 } f$ and $D _ { 2 } f$ are defined as in 5.46 except that now we allow $f$ to be a complex-valued function. Clearly $D _ { j } f = D _ { j } ( \mathbf { R e } f ) + i D _ { j } ( \mathbf { I m } f )$ for $j = 1 , 2 .$ 

11.19 Definition harmonic function
A function $u: G \to C$ on an open subset G of $R^{2}$ is called harmonic if $(D_{1}(D_{1}f))(w) + (D_{2}(D_{2}f))(w) = 0$ for all $w \in G$ . The left side of the equation above is called the Laplacian of f at w and is often denoted by $(\Delta f)(w)$ . 

## 11.20 Example harmonic functions

If $f \colon G \to \mathbf { C }$ is an analytic function on an open set $G \subset \mathbf { C }$ , then the functions Re f, Im $f , f ,$ , and $\overline { { f } }$ are all harmonic functions on $G$ , as is usually discussed near the beginning of a course on complex analysis. 

If $\boldsymbol { \zeta } \in \partial \mathbf { D }$ , then the function 

$$
w \mapsto \frac {1 - | w | ^ {2}}{| 1 - \overline {{\zeta}} w | ^ {2}}
$$

is harmonic on $\mathbf { C } \setminus \{ \zeta \}$ (see Exercise 7). 

The function $u \colon \mathbf { C } \setminus \{ 0 \} \  \ \mathbf { R }$ defined by $u ( w ) = \log | w |$ is harmonic on $\mathbf { C } \setminus \{ 0 \}$ , as you should verify. However, there does not exist a function $f$ analytic on $\mathbf { C } \setminus \{ 0 \}$ such that $u =  { \mathrm { R e } } f .$ 

The Dirichlet problem asks to extend a continuous function on the boundary of an open subset of $\bar { \mathbf { R } ^ { 2 } }$ to a function that is harmonic on the open set and continuous on the closure of the open set. Here is a more formal statement: 

Dirichlet problem on G: Suppose $G \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ is an open set and $f \colon \partial G \to \mathbf { C }$ is a continuous function. Find a continuous function $u \colon { \overline { { G } } } \to \mathbf { C }$ such that $u | _ { G }$ is harmonic and $u | _ { \partial G } = f$ 

For some open sets $G \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ , there exist continuous functions $f$ on $\partial G$ whose Dirichlet problem has no solution. However, the situation on the open unit disk D is much nicer, as we will soon see. 

The function u defined in the result below is called the Poisson integral of f on D. 

11.22 Poisson integral is harmonic
Suppose $f \in L^{1}(\partial\mathbf{D})$ . Define $u: D \to C$ by $u(rz) = (\mathcal{P}_{r}f)(z)$ for $r \in [0,1)$ and $z \in \partial D$ . Then u is harmonic on D. 

Proof If $w \in \mathbf { D }$ , then $w = r z$ for some $r \in [ 0 , 1 )$ and some $z \in \partial \mathbf { D }$ . Thus 

$$
u (w) = (\mathcal {P} _ {r} f) (z)
$$

$$
= \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \hat {f} (n) (r z) ^ {n} + \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \hat {f} (- n) (r \overline {{z}}) ^ {n}
$$

$$
= \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \hat {f} (n) w ^ {n} + \overline {{\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \overline {{\hat {f} (- n)}} w ^ {n}}}.
$$

Every function that has a power series representation on D is analytic on D. Thus the equation above shows that u is the sum of an analytic function and the complex conjugate of an analytic function. Hence u is harmonic. 

11.23 Poisson integral solves Dirichlet problem on unit disk
Suppose $f: \partial D \to C$ is continuous. Define $u: \overline{D} \to C$ by $u(rz) = \begin{cases} (\mathcal{P}_r f)(z) & \text{if } 0 \leq r < 1 \text{ and } z \in \partial D, \\ f(z) & \text{if } r = 1 \text{ and } z \in \partial D. \end{cases}$ Then u is continuous on $\overline{D}$ , $u|_{D}$ is harmonic, and $u|_{\partial D} = f$ . 

Proof Suppose $\boldsymbol { \zeta } \in \partial \mathbf { D }$ . To prove that u is continuous at $\zeta ,$ we need to show that if $w \in \overline { { \mathbf { D } } }$ is close to $\zeta ,$ , then $u ( w )$ is close to $u ( \zeta )$ . Because $u | _ { \partial \mathbf { D } } = f$ and $f$ is continuous on ∂D, we do not need to worry about the case where $w \in \partial \mathbf { D }$ . Thus assume $w \in \mathbf { D }$ . We can write $w = r z$ , where $r \in [ 0 , 1 )$ and $z \in \partial \mathbf { D }$ . Now 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {| u (\zeta) - u (w) | = | f (\zeta) - (\mathcal {P} _ {r} f) (z) |} \\ & {\qquad \leq | f (\zeta) - f (z) | + | f (z) - (\mathcal {P} _ {r} f) (z) |.} \end{array}
$$

If $w$ is close to $\zeta ,$ , then $z$ is also close to $\zeta .$ , and hence by the continuity of $f$ the first term in the last line above is small. Also, if w is close to $\zeta .$ , then $r$ is close to 1, and hence by 11.18 the second term in the last line above is small. Thus if $w$ is close to $\zeta .$ , then $u ( w )$ is close to $u ( \zeta )$ , as desired. 

The function $u | _ { \mathbf { D } }$ is harmonic on D (and hence continuous on D) by 11.22. 

The definition of u immediately implies that $u | _ { \partial \mathbf { D } } = f$ 

## Fourier Series of Smooth Functions

The Fourier series of a continuous function on ∂D need not converge pointwise (see Exercise 11). However, in this subsection we will see that Fourier series behave well for functions that are twice continuously differentiable. 

First we need to define what we mean for a function on ∂D to be differentiable. The formal definition is given below, along with the introduction of the notation $\tilde { f }$ for the transfer of $f$ to $\left( - \pi , \pi \right]$ 

$$
f ^ {[ \check {k} ]}
$$

The idea here is that we transfer a function defined on $\partial \mathbf{D}$ to $(- \pi, \pi]$ , take the usual derivative there, then transfer back to $\partial \mathbf{D}$ . 

$$
k ^ {\mathrm{th}}
$$

$$
\tilde {f}.
$$

11.24 Definition $\tilde{f}$ ; $k$ times continuously differentiable; $f^{[k]}$ Suppose $f\colon \partial \mathbf{D} \to \mathbf{C}$ is a complex-valued function on $\partial \mathbf{D}$ and $k \in \mathbf{Z}^{+} \cup \{0\}$ .

- Define $\tilde{f}\colon \mathbf{R} \to \mathbf{C}$ by $\tilde{f}(t) = f(e^{it})$ .

- $f$ is called $k$ times continuously differentiable if $\tilde{f}$ is $k$ times differentiable everywhere on $\mathbf{R}$ and its $k^{\text{th}}$ -derivative $\tilde{f}^{(k)}\colon \mathbf{R} \to \mathbf{C}$ is continuous.

- If $f$ is $k$ times continuously differentiable, then $f^{[k]}\colon \partial \mathbf{D} \to \mathbf{C}$ is defined by $f^{[k]}(e^{it}) = \tilde{f}^{(k)}(t)$ for $t \in \mathbf{R}$ . Here $\tilde{f}^{(0)}$ is defined to be $\tilde{f}$ , which means that $f^{[0]} = f$ .

Note that the function $\tilde{f}$ defined above is periodic on $\mathbf{R}$ because $\tilde{f}(t + 2\pi) = \tilde{f}(t)$ for all $t \in \mathbf{R}$ . Thus all derivatives of $\tilde{f}$ are also periodic on $\mathbf{R}$ .

11.25 Example Suppose $n \in \mathbf{Z}$ and $f\colon \partial \mathbf{D} \to \mathbf{C}$ is defined by $f(z) = z^n$ . Then $\tilde{f}\colon \mathbf{R} \to \mathbf{C}$ is defined by $\tilde{f}(t) = e^{int}$ .

If $k \in \mathbf{Z}^{+}$ , then $\tilde{f}^{(k)}(t) = i^k n^ke^{int}$ . Thus $f^{[k]}(z) = i^kn^k z^n$ for $z \in \partial \mathbf{D}$ .

Our next result gives a formula for the Fourier coefficients of a derivative.

11.26 Fourier coefficients of differentiable functions

Suppose $k \in \mathbf{Z}^{+}$ and $f\colon \partial \mathbf{D} \to \mathbf{C}$ is $k$ times continuously differentiable. Then $(f^{[k]})^{\wedge}(n) = i^kn^k\hat{f}(n)$ for every $n \in \mathbf{Z}$ .

Proof First suppose $n = 0$ . By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, we have $(f^{[k]})^{\wedge}(0) = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f^{[k]}(e^{it})\frac{dt}{2\pi} = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \tilde{f}^{(k)}(t)\frac{dt}{2\pi} = \tilde{f}^{(k-1)}(t)\bigg]_{t=-\pi}^{t=\pi} = 0$ , which is the desired result for $n = 0$ . 

Now suppose $n \in \mathbf { Z } \backslash \{ 0 \}$ . Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \big (f ^ {[ k ]} \big) ^ {\wedge} (n) = \int_ {- \pi} ^ {\pi} \tilde {f} ^ {(k)} (t) e ^ {- i n t} \frac {d t}{2 \pi} \\ \qquad = \frac {1}{2 \pi} \tilde {f} ^ {(k - 1)} (t) e ^ {- i n t} \Big ] _ {t = - \pi} ^ {t = \pi} + i n \int_ {- \pi} ^ {\pi} \tilde {f} ^ {(k - 1)} (t) e ^ {- i n t} \frac {d t}{2 \pi} \\ \qquad = i n \big (f ^ {[ k - 1 ]} \big) ^ {\wedge} (n), \end{array}
$$

where the second equality above follows from integration by parts. 

Iterating the equation above now produces the desired result. 

Now we can prove the beautiful result that a twice continuously differentiable function on ∂D equals its Fourier series, with uniform convergence of the Fourier series. This conclusion holds with the weaker hypothesis that the function is continuously differentiable, but the proof is easier with the hypothesis used here. 

11.27 Fourier series of twice continuously differentiable functions converge
Suppose $f: \partial D \rightarrow C$ is twice continuously differentiable. Then $f(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \hat{f}(n) z^{n}$ for all $z \in \partial D$ . Furthermore, the partial sums $\sum_{n=-K}^{M} \hat{f}(n) z^{n}$ converge uniformly on $\partial D$ to f as $K, M \rightarrow \infty$ . 

Proof If $n \in \mathbf { Z } \backslash \{ 0 \}$ , then 

$$
| \hat {f} (n) | = \frac {| (f ^ {[ 2 ]}) ^ {\wedge} (n) |}{n ^ {2}} \leq \frac {\| f ^ {[ 2 ]} \| _ {1}}{n ^ {2}},\tag{11.28}
$$

where the equality above follows from 11.26 and the inequality above follows from 11.9(c). Now 11.28 implies that 

$$
\sum_ {n = - \infty} ^ {\infty} | \hat {f} (n) z ^ {n} | = \sum_ {n = - \infty} ^ {\infty} | \hat {f} (n) | <   \infty\tag{11.29}
$$

for all $z \in \partial \mathbf { D }$ . The inequality above implies that $\scriptstyle \sum _ { n = - \infty } ^ { \infty } { \hat { f } } ( n ) z ^ { n }$ converges and that the partial sums converge uniformly on ∂D. 

Furthermore, for each $\mathbf { \nabla } \in \partial \mathbf { D }$ we have 

$$
f (z) = \lim _ {r \uparrow 1} \sum_ {n = - \infty} ^ {\infty} r ^ {| n |} \hat {f} (n) z ^ {n} = \sum_ {n = - \infty} ^ {\infty} \hat {f} (n) z ^ {n},
$$

where the first equality holds by 11.18 and 11.11, and the second equality holds by the Dominated Convergence Theorem (use counting measure on $\mathbf { Z } )$ and 11.29. 

In 1923 Andrey Kolmogorov (1903–1987) published a proof that there exists a function in $L ^ { 1 } ( \partial { \bf D } )$ whose Fourier series diverges almost everywhere on ∂D. Kolmogorov’s result and the result in Exercise 11 probably led most mathematicians to suspect that there exists a continuous function on ∂D whose Fourier series diverges almost everywhere. However, in 1966 Lennart Carleson (1928–) showed that if $f \in L ^ { 2 } ( \partial \mathbf { D } )$ (and in particular if f is continuous on ∂D), then the Fourier series of f converges to f almost everywhere.
